speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday last the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) put the following question to me:
Has the minister explored the possibility of using the dams north of Ottawa to hold back a greater head of water to alleviate flood conditions?
The answer is that the officials of the Department of Public Works, aided by outside consultants, have given a great deal of thought to this problem. To date they have found no way of doing more to alleviate flood conditions. I have in hand a comprehensive report and study concerning this question, which I propose to read.
The question of controlling the flow of the Ottawa river has been studied by the Department of Public Works for many years, in consultation with the two provincial power commissions operating the river and with the other industries, including lumbering, who utilize the river for navigation. The study has not only been carried out by our engineers; we have added thereto engineers who are fully familiar with the situation. We retain on our staff a consulting engineer who knows the situation particularly well and whose guidance has been followed' for many years, as well as in the present situation. Any steps taken to guide and control the present floods were as directed by him.
On further going over the situation and analysing it thoroughly, it is agreed that no other course could have been followed that would have made flood conditions in the Ottawa area any less difficult. This opinion is shared by the officers of the power companies, of the two provincial power commissions and of the other services utilizing the river. In considering the question of the control of water at different dams, the first point always kept in mind is to alleviate flood conditions as far as possible, and the
80709-145J
second is the storage of water to be used later by the different parties. In detail there are on the river between Ottawa and the headwaters dams both for power and for storage, as follows:
Dozois: built and operated by the Quebec Hydro Electric Commission. This has a drainage area of 3,000 square miles. At the beginning of the present freshet season this reservoir was completely empty, but was closed by the Quebec authorities on March 31, and has remained closed ever since. The flow into this reservoir during the past two weeks has exceeded over 20,000 cubic feet per second.
2.	Rapid No. 7: operated by the Quebec government. This is a power and storage development. To date, with a limited outflow required for power purposes only and the main dam closed, it has not been completely refilled.
3.	Quinze reservoir:	controlled by the
Department of Public Works. Drainage basin 8,900 square miles. At the start of the present freshet this reservoir was entirely empty, and on April 16 it was partly closed and only sufficient water permitted through this dam-approximately 7,500 cubic feet for power purposes.
4.	Timiskaming reservoir: dam operated by the Department of Public Works. Drainage area, 17,000 square miles. At the start of the freshet this reservoir was entirely open. At the beginning of the freshet the run-off increased the water level with the discharge fully open and the lake rose seven feet. On April 17 in order to reduce the flood the dam was partially closed. This resulted in the reservoir rising over one-half a foot in one day, which would have filled the reservoir in a few days and resulted in a higher outflow than at present is being encountered. It was necessary to keep lake Timiskaming open, as by its own drainage area it went up one foot in one day, and with rises like this apparent it is certain that conditions on lake Timiskaming would be such that the sewage disposal and filtration plants of the towns of both Haileybury and New Liskeard, which always have to be watched, would have been flooded out.
From Timiskaming to Ottawa there are the following dams: 1. La Cave, under development; 2. Des Joachims, now fully developed; 3. Bryson, fully developed; 4.

Flood Conditions
Chenaux, fully developed; 5. Chats falls, fully developed; 6. Chaudiere, fully developed.
In the area covered by these six developments there is the run-off from approximately
17,000	square miles, which accumulates a discharge of approximately 145,000 cubic feet per second, none of which can be controlled at any of the dams, as there is absolutely no storage.
It is therefore evident that the whole situation so far as the vicinity of Ottawa is concerned was due to the inability to store any of the waters between Timiskaming and Ottawa, a distance of approximately 200 miles, and that therefore the major lakes, Timiskaming, Quinze and Dozois, had no effect on the flood that took place in the Ottawa river, but, on the contrary, assisted in retarding the flow.
All things considered, we know of no move that could have been made that would alleviate flood conditions in the area other than the ones that have been indicated and we are pleased to have had the cooperation of the Ontario and Quebec hydroelectric power commissions in order to give full effect to these measures.

INTERNATIONAL
speechtext: What action has the Minister of Justice taken respecting the report of the commissioner of the Combines Investigation Act, dated October 10, 1945, and entitled "Canada and International Cartels"?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: INTERNATIONAL
speechtext:
In a reply which I made on December 5, 1949, in regard to action taken with respect to recommendations contained in the report "Canada and International Cartels", a summary was given of the position at that time, and, I shall now restate the substance of that reply with the minor changes necessary to bring it up to date.
The recommendations made in the report "Canada and International Cartels" are set out in pages 66 to 69, and may be summarized as follows:
1.	Particular attention should be given by the combines investigation commission to restrictive agreements based on patents.
The Combines Investigation Act was amended in 1946 to give powers to the exchequer court to issue remedial orders in cases of use of patents or trade-marks unduly to limit production or restrain or injure trade. In its inquiries the combines investigation commission gives particular attention to restrictive arrangements based on patents.
2.	The establishment of official government records which would show from time to time any significant change in the degree of financial control which corporations outside Canada exercise over individual domestic companies.
Information with respect to this matter is compiled by the dominion bureau of statistics which, from time to time, publishes the result of its studies in this field.
3.	More adequate provision for the initiation of inquiries by the combines investigation commission into restraints of trade and unfair trade practices.
Amendments made to the Combines Investigation Act in 1946 empowered the commissioner to receive and inquire into complaints respecting practices alleged to be offences under the act or under sections 498 and 498A of the Criminal Code. Provision was also made in the 1946 amendments to restore the power of the commissioner to initiate inquiries under section 12 of the act.
4.	The building up of an effective organization under the Combines Investigation Act supported by sufficient appropriations.
The staff of the commission is now thirty-one, compared with an average of eight in 1945. Recruitment of several additional officers is currently proceeding through the civil service commission. Appropriations have increased from $61,000 in the fiscal year 1945-46 to $237,669 in the fiscal year 1950-51.
Questions
Estimates for the current year are slightly in excess of the 1950-51 appropriations.
5.	Support should be given by the government of Canada to the establishment of an international office to deal with international cartels.
Canada participated in the United Nations conferences on trade and employment which resulted in the Havana charter for an international trade organization. This charter contained provisions for dealing with restrictive business practices by cartels. The charter has not been ratified by the requisite number of countries to bring it into effect.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate on the budget has been going on for some time. We have heard a number of speakers, and most of the addresses have been extremely interesting. All subjects can be discussed in the budget debate, except of course the $65 million wheat payment, on which discussion is prohibited. It is natural that both in the house and in the country there should be much interest in the budget, and it is only right that many hon. members should discuss it. It touches the lives of all our people; its effects are felt in all homes and all businesses across the country. It affects people's pleasure; it affects every phase and every walk of life. To some the budget means privation; to others it simply means the curtailing of some of their pleasures and perhaps a few of their necessities.
As I listened to the debate I noticed that most of the government members more or less praised the budget and picked out what they felt was of benefit to the government. Those in the opposition of course have criticized it, and deservedly so; to my mind it is open to much criticism. It does emphasize the fact that we are living in most strenuous times, as is indicated by (he budgets !Mr. McHraith.l

of other countries-Great Britain, France, Italy, the United States.
We have of course the fighting in Korea, which again seems to have become intensified. We have the cold war all over the world, the war of nerves, which also seems to be gaining in momentum. In addition we have in the United States a sort of civil war of words. This is something which I think must give the people in many parts of the world some cause for worry. We in Canada have always been proud to be associated with the United States as we are today. But I think we realize, as do other countries, that world leadership is something which is more or less new to our friends to the south, and that perhaps they are not as experienced as they should be in the role of world leaders. We regret, of course, that the British commonwealth of nations, which in the last two wars was more or less the leader in war and world matters, today is not in a position to fill that role, I believe the people of Canada are willing to pay their full share to meet the needs arising from world conditions, but I also feel that we should like to know just where we are going. We have been disturbed over the situation in the United States during the last week, and the people of Canada hope, as do the people in many other countries, that world affairs will not be determined by political expediency in the United States, a country which should be giving leadership- we hope it will give it-in matters of this kind.
The amount we are asked for in the budget, $3,700 million, is an enormous sum of money. Of this, over $1,664 million is to be used for defence. We realize that large sums must be spent for defence. The part we are taking now in the Korean war; the part which we must take, and indeed are pledged to take, with regard to the Atlantic pact and Atlantic defence; the part we must take in developing the defence of our own country, and also the part we must take in carrying on the general services of our country-all these make us realize that the appropriation of large sums is necessary.
A moment ago I pointed out that people in other parts of the world as well are being heavily taxed. I do not suppose that any other people are carrying a heavier burden or are more heavily taxed than the people of Great Britain. I mention this fact, Mr. Speaker, because it has been disconcerting to read recently in some of the papers-not in this country but in the United States-comment to the effect that Great Britain is not carrying her load. It might interest hon. members to know that neither Canada nor the United States can compare with Great Britain in the

matter of the weight of taxation which is imposed upon the people. I should like to give a few instances.
A low-priced car in Great Britain pays a tax of $1,180. The tax on gasoline in Great Britain is 50 cents a gallon, as compared with 134 cents paid here in Canada. We feel that we are paying an enormous tax on cigarettes, and so we are; but in Great Britain there is a tax of 52 cents on twenty cigarettes as compared with 25 cents in Canada. One could go on giving instances which indicate the great burden these people in the old country are bearing at the present time.
Britain is raising $13 billion in three years for defence. When we are told that she is not carrying her load, we need only to point out that she already has four divisions in Europe, whereas we in Canada have no troops there at all. She already has over a division in Korea. In Malaya she has troops which have been fighting now for a considerable length of time. She has troops in Hong Kong, in Iran, in Egypt, indeed in all parts of the world. This will give some idea of the burden which is being borne by that country. Since we are being asked to raise this enormous sum of money, I think the chief concern of the people in Canada today is that the money may be fairly collected from those who are most able to pay. Our second matter of concern is that this money must not be wasted but must be economically spent, and, third, we hope that the government will be able to stop inflation.
In discussing this matter in his budget speech on April 10, the minister said, as reported at page 1797 of Hansard:
In the months that lie ahead, perhaps indeed for several years, we shall face a test of nerves, of our readiness to sacrifice immediate interests for future security. This is the background against which the budget must be viewed.
Contending that his policies were antiinflationary, he declared, as reported at page 1800 of Hansard:
The essential principle in preventing inflation is to restrict the total of all expenditure, public and private, to an amount which can be met from our production and imports.
This may be sound economics, but it is unlikely to impress the average individual who thinks of inflation in terms of skyrocketing prices and1 cannot see how it will be checked by imposts such as the boost in the sales tax, which will hoist prices even higher and make it more difficult for families in the modest income brackets to secure the necessities of life. The theory is, of course, that private spending can be controlled by taxes heavy enough to balance the amount of money in circulation against the supply of goods
The Budget-Mr. Brooks available; but it does not hold water. The surplus cash raked in by the treasury is quickly distributed again in lavish government expenditures.
Some may be encouraged by the fact that the minister mentioned the need for restricting public spending as well as private. It is to be hoped that this was not merely ar, empty statement.
All Canadians realize it is imperative that the country rearm, and that this will involve tremendous expenditures, but the revenue from the new taxes should be earmarked strictly for defence, and all non-essential government expenditures should be cut to the bone.
Speaking of the sales tax, Mr. Speaker, I should like to indicate its effect not upon the people of Canada in general, but more particularly upon the people of my own province. I do not know whether it is generally known or not, but besides the federal sales tax, in New Brunswick we have a four per cent sales tax-not on essential foods, but on all other articles in general. Therefore this ten per cent federal sales tax becomes fourteen per cent in New Brunswick, and when you consider the tax on the tax on the tax, as was pointed out here the other day by the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), the sales tax in our small province becomes something in the vicinity of twenty per cent. This is a burden which is very difficult indeed for our people to bear, and no relief of any kind seems to be in sight.
I should like to consider the tax on electric goods. I can best illustrate how this tax bears on the young people, as has been mentioned in this house a number of times, by reciting an experience I had over the week end. I happened to be in the city of Montreal, and I met a young man and a young woman from my own constituency, who had left their home in New Brunswick a little over a year ago. I asked them how they were making out. They are married and have a child. They explained to me that for the past year they have been living in two rooms, but that they had hoped to get better accommodation. The cheapest they could get that was suitable was $75 a month, and they said that they had planned to buy an electric stove, and they also wished to have a refrigerator and some household furniture. They had arranged to buy and pay for these different articles, but now they find that the price of the electric stove they wished to buy has gone up fifteen per cent. The refrigerator they intended to buy has gone up fifteen per cent. There is a tax on the furniture that they intended to purchase,

The Budget-Mr. Brooks and the budget which they had been operating on for the past year has now been knocked on the head, as it were, and these young people, like many thousands of others across this country, are very much concerned. They had hoped that they might buy these articles on the instalment plan, but the instalments have now been restricted by the government, and this also has upset their plans.
Another matter which the people are very much concerned about is the question of government savings. We are told time and time again that it is very difficult for members of the opposition to point out just how savings can be made in government administration. [DOT]Not knowing all the facts about the expenditures of the government, it is very difficult indeed to point specifically to individual items. Last year an hon. member spoke about savings in government publications. That is something we can all see, because day after day and week after week, whether we are in this House of Commons or whether we are at home, we receive publications from the different departments of this government, publications which are too numerous for us to read. Most of them go into the wastepaper basket. I am satisfied that the hon. member who brought this matter before the house last year was justified in saying that it was nothing but a waste of money and an unnecessary expenditure. To my mind, Mr. Speaker, these publications are nothing more or less than pamphlets for the glorification of this government, and for propaganda purposes, and they could very well be done away with.
There is also the question of reduction in staffs. This matter has been discussed in the house. In the old days, days not so long ago, most staffs were here in the city of Ottawa. We had of course a postmaster, a man in charge of the customs and a few public servants scattered about the country; but today in every village and every town across this country there is a staff of government employees. I am not saying that they should be discharged, but there should be some investigation, as there has been in the United States, to find out if all these employees are necessary.
Last week I received a letter from a man in my constituency. He had applied for the war veterans allowance. It was a clear case. There was no reason why he should not be entitled to the war veterans allowance, but over a period of three months as many as four different government officials called on this man to make sure whether he was entitled to the war veterans allowance. This sort of thing is going on all over the country.


As I said a moment ago, we should look into the question of government employees and see if many on the staffs could not be cut down.
So far as transportation is concerned there have been many changes in comparatively recent years. I recall that in my own province twenty-five or thirty years ago we had ten or a dozen steamers plying up and down the Saint John river, for instance, and its tributaries. It was practically the only means of transportation. Today there is not a large steamer on the Saint John river. The work is all done by trucks. What applies to the Saint John river I am satisfied applies to many other rivers and lakes across the country. But we still have the same expense. There are dozens of lighthouses on the river and tributaries. I have been told by many who live up the Saint John river that practically the only boats they have there are little pleasure yachts, small tugs, and so on. It seems to me this is something which should be investigated by the Minister of Transport with a view to seeing whether some savings could not be effected.
On the question of radar, I remember that when we visited the national research council last year we were told that while radar had been used previously on large steamers, through invention and science they now find that it is possible to make cheaper radar sets which can be used oni small pleasure boats and on small tugs. I understand they are also being used on fishing boats. It is likely that a great saving could be made if this question were investigated with a view to adopting safe and up-to-date aids to transportation and doing away with outdated methods.
I see the hon. member for Inverness-Rich-mond (Mr. Carroll) in his seat, and I should like to make one or two comments on his speech of a few days ago-it has been referred to already by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis). The hon. member for Inverness-Richmond is very fortunate- indeed he is more fortunate than most of us from the maritime provinces, and perhaps for that reason he can look in a more detached manner upon our situation down there. A few days ago he said that the people of the maritime provinces were more or less to blame for the situation in which they found themselves.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that the hon. member is following in the footsteps of the hon. member for Cape Breton South.
I did not discuss the maritime provinces at all in connection with confederation and industries. My sole theme was the province of Nova Scotia.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is a queer thing to me if Nova Scotia is not a maritime province. What applies to Nova Scotia applies also to New Brunswick and to Prince Edward Island, or to any of the four maritime provinces. The hon. member was speaking about Nova Scotia, and he made light of the decentralization of industry. He said it would be foolhardy for anyone to stand in his place and say that governments or government policies could have anything to do with the decentralization of industry, and contended that it was entirely a matter for the provinces.
I agree with the hon. member that it is not possible for this or any other government to go to a large concern and say: you must send part of your factory down to New Brunswick, or Nova Scotia, as the case may be. We do not say that, nor do we believe it. But we do say, as was pointed out the other day, that before confederation the people of the maritime provinces were prosperous, and after confederation dozens, yes hundreds of industries, left the maritimes and came to central Canada. We contend that it was policies of the federal government which caused the loss of industries in the maritime provinces.
We are not asking this or any other government to force individual companies to send branches to the maritimes, but we are asking that freight rates, fiscal policies, and other matters under the control of the federal government be handled in such a way that it will be profitable for industries to disperse their plants and to go into the maritime provinces. It was the policy of the federal government which drove them out, and we believe a policy can be evolved which will send them back.
Let me point out some of the disadvantages of centralization. If the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) is in his seat, he will recall that for many years there was in the town of St. Stephen a soap factory. A few years ago Lever Brothers obtained what amounted almost to a monopoly of the soap industry in this country, with the result that the factory was closed and was moved to Ontario. This meant less purchasing power in St. Stephen. It meant a loss of business; it meant that those whose employment depended on that factory had to take their families away. That is one of the results of of centralization.
Then let me illustrate the principle of decentralization. Only last year it was decided to build a cement factory in my constituency of Royal, at a place called Havelock, with the result that today the Canada Cement Company is building a plant there. It will

The Budget-Mr. Brooks employ about three hundred persons. The village today has a bank and a theatre; it has enlarged its schools; the merchants are prosperous, and the farmers of the area have a market in which to dispose of their goods. That is what decentralization means, Mr. Speaker. As I said a moment ago, we had a bitter experience with centralization.
I should like to discuss for a few moments an item which appeared in the press a few days ago with regard to an interview given by a member of the Nova Scotia legislature who was paying a visit to Florida and reported in the Florida press. Had he been an ordinary visitor the press and the people of Canada would have disregarded it. However, since he was a member of the Nova Scotia government there was more inclination to take his remarks seriously. The press report states that Mr. Harold Connolly, on his visit to Florida, predicted the union of Canada and the United States within a quarter of a century. I believe I know as well as anyone the people of the maritime provinces, particularly those in my own section, and I would say that not ten per cent of them want Canada to become part of the United States. He went on to say, as indicated in the press report:
The people of Canada have a greater affinity for the United States than for Britain.
I do not know where he gets his information. The report continues to quote him as follows:
The people of these two countries speak the same language, think along the same lines . . .
In Canada we speak two languages, both French and English; and I am satisfied that if within twenty-five years we became part of the United States we would not retain those two languages; rather we would all speak one language, what might be called the American language.
I have referred to this matter because I feel that Mr. Connolly was talking through his hat-or perhaps he was affected by the extreme heat of Florida, in contrast with the cold climate of Nova Scotia.

The determination of Canadians to retain a distinct national culture, and their hope of thereby providing a strong link between the United States and Britain, were expressed here today by Prof. Robert J. Love, who is head of the department of education at the university of New Brunswick and was addressing a group of students and educational leaders at the conference on Canadian-American affairs being held here under the sponsorship of the university of Maine.
Then the report quotes Professor Love in these words:
"There were many influences of the United States on Canada, but we are distinctly Canadian and intend to stay so," he said. "We want to stay Canadian, not because we don't like the United States, but because we feel we can accomplish more, contribute more, on that basis." He went on to point out that one of Canada's particular contributions would be to act as a strong bond between the United Kingdom and the United States.
In my opinion that expresses the situation quite clearly as to how we feel in Canada. .
In closing I should like to refer to a matter that particularly affects my constituency. In the course of this debate we have heard some excellent addresses on dairying in Canada. We regret the position in which the dairy interests of this country find themselves. This is so particularly in the valley of the Kennebecasis in New Brunswick.

In my constituency of Royal, one of the finest dairying counties in eastern Canada, and I think one of the finest in all Canada. There are three large butter factories in my constituency. There is the Sussex Cheese and Butter Company; there is the Millstream dairy, and there is the Harvey dairy at Hampstead on the Saint John river. The butter factory at Sussex had the distinction a few years ago of making more butter
fMr. Dickey.]
in one season than any other factory in Canada. That will give hon. members some idea of the extent to which our part of the country is interested in dairying. The town of Sussex, my home town, has been known as the buttermilk town.
What the hon. member for Hastings-Peter-borough (Mr. White) and the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) pointed out with regard to their constituencies is true also of our part of the country. Because of the high prices obtainable for dairy cattle,, many farmers have been selling their herds, with the result that there is not as much dairying going on. Many young men who are purchasing farms with the idea of going into dairying find it almost impossible to buy dairy cattle today, because they cannot afford to pay $300 or $400 a head for them. A total of 47,000 were sent to the United States last year and, practically the same number the year before. Many thousands more will be sent this year, with the result that dairy herds will be considerably depleted in some parts of the country.
The dairy industry is suffering severely from these conditions. I should like to advocate what was advocated by the hon. member for Lanark, that something be done in this connection, that a floor price of 62 cents be placed under butter as requested by the dairying industry. I hope that the Minister of Agriculture and the government as a whole will give serious consideration to this matter, which is so important to dairy farmers of my constituency as well as to the dairying interests across Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am going to do my best
to enlighten the hon. member, if that is possible, during the course of this speech.
In his budget speech the Minister of Finance gave a comprehensive review of the

economic position of this nation. He indicated the steady growth that Canada has undergone since the end of the war. He indicated the financial measures which the government feel they must take in order to pay for our greatly increased defence expenditures and to take part in the joint defence of freedom to which this country is committed.
I think the people of the country appreciate that the budget is a tough but realistic one. Actually I think they expected it to be much more severe. I think they appreciate that the Minister of Finance had laid a heavy load on the people of this country but it has been laid fairly. To my mind no better evidence of this statement can be found than what was contained in the leading editorial of the Toronto Telegram the day after the budget presentation. As hon. members know, the Toronto Telegram is the one true blue, unswerving champion of the Progressive Conservative party. This editorial starts off as follows:
Budget lays Heavy but Even Burden
As a budget designed to raise revenue on a fair basis to pay for defence costs that all recognize must be met. Mr. Abbott has done a creditable job.
Then they go on to analyse the various proposals in the budget, and they conclude with the following words:
In laying a heavy burden on the Canadian taxpayer Mr. Abbott has judged that the country realizes the need for a strong defence, and in the main he has laid the burden evenly on everyone's shoulders.
Since the introduction of the budget various members of the opposition have criticized certain of the tax proposals. Those of us who sat in the budget committee knew long before the budget was introduced into the house from what direction these attacks would come. The C.C.F., of course, would criticize the corporation tax, that we were not soaking the companies enough. Both parties would recoil in horror from any increase in the personal income tax. They would decry our policy not to increase taxes on that luxury, liquor, and at the same time they would oppose our putting increased taxes on those necessities, cigarettes. They would call the cut in the tax on candy appeasement of the children. We knew that the tax on electrical appliances would be labelled by the opposition as a blow to the Canadian home. Above all, we knew that the two per cent increase in sales tax would never be referred to as a two per cent increase but as a twenty-five per cent increase.
We knew these things would come, because the function of an opposition is always to oppose all tax measures and never to suggest any alternative tax measures. Let me turn, therefore, to each of these items.
The Budget-Mr. Sinclair
First, let me recall to hon. members that the task facing the Minister of Finance this year was to raise an extra $400 million to meet those defence costs which have been so thoroughly endorsed by members of this House of Commons. The primary purpose of this budget is to raise revenues; the secondary purpose of these tax measures is to curb unnecessary spending in order to make goods and materials more available for defence needs. In this task the minister has tried to spread as fairly as possible the load upon the Canadian people.
Let me turn first to the corporation tax. That, of course, was the field of main attack by the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell). At the end of the war we had an 18 per cent corporation tax, plus a 100 per cent excess profits tax. That was changed later to a flat 30 per cent corporation tax which was applied to all the profits of corporations. Later, as a measure of encouragement to small companies, we changed that tax to 10 per cent on the first $10,000 of profits, and to make sure that the country did not lose revenue because of this change we increased the tax on the bigger corporations to 33 per cent. That was the tax in effect on corporations of this country at the time of the Korean aggression. The baby budget last fall provided for an increase in taxes to meet added defence costs, one being an increase of 5 per cent in corporation taxes as well as a substantial increase in the liquor taxes. The corporation tax was then 15 per cent on small companies and 38 per cent on big companies, plus the 5 per cent tax which we collect for eight of the provinces, and in the case of Quebec and Ontario plus the 7 per cent tax which they levy. Now, again to meet still added defence costs, the minister has imposed a surcharge of 20 per cent on this corporation tax rate.
Why a surcharge? There are good reasons for a surcharge instead of another change in the rates. In the first place it leaves the existing tax structure unaltered. Whatever tax is payable under the old plan, in the end 20 per cent more is payable. The second reason I think is good psychology; it is that every corporation

and the same applies to individuals-in making out its tax return may have again impressed upon it the cost.of the defence program, because this is a defence surcharge. If conditions in the world improve that 20 per cent surcharge can be lowered. If conditions get worse it may be necessary to increase it. We did not put the surcharge on the small corporations; but that now lifts the corporation tax payable in Canada to 50-6 per cent on gross profits in eight of the provinces and to 52-6 per cent in the two central provinces, where incidentally most of
2276	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Sinclair the corporations are located. This means that in Canada today we are taking more than half the gross profits of the corporations. It means in effect that the people of Canada are the major shareholders in every successful corporation. Of course if they do not make money it is their own money they lose, but we are now taking more than half the profits of the successful corporations of Canada.
The leader of the C.C.F. party asserts that we should be taking still more. He complains of rising profits, and suggests that a cut in those profits would mean a cut in prices. I am indebted to the editor of the Montreal Gazette for calling to my attention an excellent publication put out by the British Labour party entitled "This cost of living business." You know, over in Britain the socialists are in power, and they have the same problems as far as inflation is concerned as the Liberals have in this country. The publication to which I refer is not a government publication. It is not an official publication of the Labour party. It is * pamphlet turned out for the benefit of their supporters, so they may have some of the answers to give the people who are complaining about this high cost of living. I would recommend the pamphlet to every hon. member of this house, because it will show the difference between the thinking of the socialists who are in power and socialists who are not in power. You will realize, of course, that the British Labour government, like the socialist government in Saskatchewan, have learned some bitter lessons while in power. In Saskatchewan they learned those lessons through their boot factory and their blanket factory. In Britain they learned them through the ground nuts scheme in Tanganyika and the poultry scheme in Gambia. The portion of this pamphlet to which I want to direct particular attention, however, is the part relating to profits. All hon. members have heard the socialists in this country denounce the profit motive. They would work for production for use, not for profit. The socialists of Britain were no different until they got into power, but this is what the pamphlet says:
Profits cater for the creation of reserves to pay for expansion and re-equipment, and the additional money manufacturers want to pay dividends to their shareholders. The more money firms put aside to develop new methods of production, the more consumers have to pay now for goods. But new equipment and better laid-out factories mean more efficient production, lower costs, and the possibility of lower prices in the long run. If the money to pay for this were not raised from profits it would have to be raised in some other way.


Something most of us knew a long time ago.
When prices are rising, and both production and sales increasing as at present, profits are likely to be relatively high and rising. This is not to say that ail firms or all industries will be making profits. Most consumer goods are made by a fairly large number of firms, the profits of which vary between the leading and the less efficient firms.
Profits tax prevents the accumulation of excessive profits. The proceeds of this taxation help to pay for food subsidies, social services and other instruments of community welfare.
Then what can be done in reference to limiting profits?
Can we, then, cut profits?
First, it has been explained that, to the extent that profit makes provision for re-equipment and new building, it is an element in increasing efficiency in industry which, in the long run, should make price reduction possible. This leaves then that part of the profit which is distributed to shareholders.
A reduction in distributed profits could do little to reduce prices. They are a very small part of the cost of any item so, although there are very many excellent reasons for dividend limitation and profit control, their effectiveness as a means of reducing the cost of living is not one of them. Even if profits were eliminated altogether there would still be a cost of living problem.
If the leader of the C.C.F. does not want to learn from the experience of the Labour government in London, I have another suggestion to offer. It is a suggestion I have made in the past. I am always amazed that those who speak for the socialist party about business, business profits, corporation taxes and so on, are those who have had absolutely no experience with them. I would like to see the leader of the C.C.F. party put up the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) or the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Jones), both extremely successful businessmen, and let us have their views on whether or not we are taxing corporations enough. Let us have their views on whether it is possible for business to evade taxes or to ease the burden. I make it a point, of course, to talk to as many people in business as I can and get their reaction to tax changes, and I have spoken to the hon. member for Moose Jaw.
I am sure he will not think I am abusing any confidence when I say he gave me a new wrinkle after the last tax change went through. He said, "Abbott is now the major shareholder in my company. He takes 50-6 per cent of the profits, and more than that he takes it in cash payable immediately. I am left with accounts receivable, stock on hand and the investment I put into the business."
The next point is this matter of the limit of 5 per cent, which the leader of the C.C.F. also criticizes; that is, that the surtax should not cut the profits of any corporation to less

than 5 per cent of the capital employed. The reason for this is very simple. There are corporations in this country whose profits are limited by federal, provincial or municipal regulation. I refer to the group of corporations generally called public utilities. Their profits are limited; the rates they can charge are tied in with the profits, and when we levy a heavy tax rate on corporations like that of course we greatly reduce their earning power. That is a bad thing if at the same time we are expecting those companies to expand. Today, with defence needs what they are, we are expecting the power companies of this country to greatly expand their facilities for the production of electrical power. We are expecting these corporations to improve their transportation facilities. That requires more capital. They certainly are not going to get it from profits, because their profits are limited, and since we have increased the tax they have great difficulty borrowing in the open market. Who will put money into a corporation where the profits are so limited when he can just as easily put it into other industrial stocks which are making higher profits? That is the reason we have this safeguard that the surtax shall not reduce the profits of those public utilities corporations to less than 5 per cent.
The third point in connection with corporation taxation is this change in depreciation, this deferred depreciation. It is a direct consequence of the fact that we are now taking more than half the profits of a corporation. Once we do that we cross a psychological barrier and get into the field of excess profits tax thinking. The businessman thinks the government is taking more than half his money. Then, of course, he is an easy victim to those salesmen who try to load him up with every type of frill for his business, electric typewriters, fancy chrome fronts and all that sort of thing, with the thought that the government is going to pay for half of it out of profits and the depreciation will take care of the rest. It was to stop needless expansion of unessential industry at this time that the minister announced this plan, not to halt depreciation but to postpone depreciation on such items for four years. The choice is the choice of the individual businessman. If he chooses to go ahead, that is his choice; but he will get no depreciation on it until the four years are up. Curiously enough the British, in their budget presented the same day, arrived at almost the same device to halt needless expenditure in unessential business.
I should like to finish this corporation tax with just one other item for the leader of the C.C.F. party. Actually Canada taxes
The Budget-Mr. Sinclair corporations much more heavily than does the Labour party in Great Britain. Until this budget the British had a tax of 30 per cent on distributed profits, that is dividends paid out. In the last budget, that was raised to 50 per cent. We, however, have this tax today of 50-6 per cent on all profits paid out or not. If they are paid out as dividends, they then become subject to the personal income tax which ranges from 15 per cent in the first bracket to 80 per cent in the top bracket. If the eventual recipient of those dividends dies, then we take another crack at it in the form of very heavy succession duties. On the other hand, if the corporation itself chooses to keep half of those profits in the form of adding to the capital, we charge them 15 per cent.
I turn now to the personal income tax and the 20 per cent surcharge. It was put on for exactly the same reasons as I mentioned in connection with the corporate tax. It would not alter the existing tax structure, but it would be a constant reminder to every Canadian that the defence of freedom is not free. There is a price that we must pay for these things. Of course, we expected an immediate revival of the exemptions bidding and criticism of our political opponents as we had later in 1949. We had the Tories bidding $1,200 and $2,400 in 1949, and we had the C.C.F. bidding $1,500 and $3,000 as exemptions under personal income tax. Those bids have been repeated. The only interesting thing about it is that the member for Hastimgs-Peterborough became a little confused and though a Tory he made the C.C.F. bid of $1,500 and $3,000.
I should like to turn now to the subject of the surtax and those exemptions. The most curious charge in connection with the surtax was made by the leader of the C.C.F. (Mr. Coldwell) and the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) when they said it was not progressive. This is not just progressive, it is violently progressive.. We will take an example of $100 of taxable income in the first bracket and then in the top bracket. In the first bracket, $100 at the old rate of 15 per cent will take $15 out of the hundred leaving him $85 income. At the new rate, with 20 per cent surcharge added, he pays $18 tax. He is left with $82, so he has suffered a cut in income from $85 to $82, 3-5 per cent. Let us take $100 in the top bracket, the 80 per cent bracket. Under the old tax rate a man had $20 left. We increased the 80 per cent by 20 per cent to make it 96 per cent, so he is left with $4. In other words, the income he received has been reduced from $20 to $4, am 80 per cent reduction in his income. That is not just progressive, it is so violently progressive
HOiJSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Sinclair that, as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) pointed out in his budget speech, we cannot go on with that level of surcharge. If it is necessary to raise additional taxes there will have to be a change in the base rate.
I should like to consider the commodity taxes now. To start off, of course, there is liquor. Hon. members generally, except the Conservatives, deplored the fact that we had not increased the tax on liquor. An expression used was that liquor was going scot-free. I want to tell you today that liquor is one commodity on which we have never reduced the taxation, even in the glorious days of the sunshine budget. Liquor was the first commodity we hit in the baby budget. Today a bottle of rye whisky which the distiller sells to the liquor control board for $1.10 costs the consumer $4.25, a 300 per cent mark-up on the manufacturer's cost; that is certainly not "scot-free". We have felt from an examination of our tax records that the point of diminishing returns has almost been reached so far as the liquor tax is concerned. It is aggravated by the condition that there is such a disparity between the cost of manufacture and the cost of sale, and when the actual manufacture is a fairly simple process. You always have the threat of widespread bootlegging and moonshining. It was for these reasons that in this budget liquor was left untouched.
If we had any doubts about how right our position was, it was certainly put at ease by a statement made by Premier Frost, who after all is the only Conservative premier in Canada today, and is generally regarded as' the white hope of the party. In the legislature in Queen's Park, he had this to say about the liquor tax:
My own preference would be in favour of the federal government making some suitable arrangements to vacate the liquor tax field, so that the provinces would not only have the problems but the revenues. Indeed, I now express the hope that the federal government will make a start by not imposing new taxes in this field.
Then he added later:
The province of Ontario might be pushed into a $10 million deficit by further federal taxation of liquor.
Then later he added:
I have expressed these views to the Minister of Finance and others, and have stated them publicly, and I take this opportunity of reaffirming my position.
Well, that was one of the reasons why the liquor tax was not increased.
I have had much pleasure in sitting as a listener during the last two dominion-provincial conferences. I think one of the great tributes which can be paid to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is the harmony
(Mr. Sinclair.]

which now exists between the federal government and the ten provinces. It was for that reason there was no consideration at all given in this budget to moving into some of the joint fields in which we were during the last war, such as the amusement tax, parimutuel tax and gasoline tax. At the moment we are leaving those to the provinces. Mind you, this is not a tax matter so far as the provinces are concerned. They are in the business of selling liquor just as any other concern who is in business in Canada selling any commodity. They are appealing to us for tax relief in the same way as any other business group comes to the Minister of Finance and puts forward special pleas as to why their commodity should not be hurt so far as extra taxes are concerned.
There was another reason which I think would not have affected the thinking of the Minister of Finance but which is in the background as far as such members as myself are concerned. Suppose we had increased the liquor tax and Premier Frost, who is also the provincial treasurer, had had a deficit of $10 million: we might have been accused of deliberately dulling the lustre of the only good leader the Tories have in the field at the present time. We have preferred to leave that job to the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Thomson), who will do that job this year.
Taking candy as the next item, we had tangible evidence of the law of diminishing returns here. In the baby budget we imposed a 30 per cent tax on candy. The candy manufacturers were able to show through their sales, and the Department of National Revenue could see from the tax collections, that the tax was too severe in relation to the tax on other industries. They were suffering a steady loss of income. It was for that reason that the tax was cut from 30 per cent to 15 per cent. It has always been the intention of the Minister of Finance to spread the tax load fairly across all industries. If a mistake is made, it will be corrected, as we have corrected this.
The excise taxes are the next group, and I think there is fairly general agreement that the increase in tax from 15 per cent to 25 per cent on luxuries and semi-luxuries was necessary. There was, of course, a protest on the special 15 per cent tax increase on electric stoves, refrigerators and washing machines. Well, that tax was imposed, first of all, for the same primary reason as other taxes, for revenue. The second reason was to check spending on goods with defence content. The spending on these items has been amazing in the last few years. The Minister of Finance put on the record some of the increases in sales in individual goods,

not dollar sales. Refrigerator sales, for example, last year were double the previous year and three times the year before. These articles, of course, are articles which do use a great deal of material which is extremely necessary for defence. We think of steel first of all. There is another one, though, copper. Some of you may have seen the quite striking advertisement appearing in most of the United States magazines this month, by the Anaconda Copper Company, the greatest primary producer of copper in the United States and one which generally does not advertise in consumer magazines. The advertisement is headed:
How many rounds can your kitchen shoot?
Then they go on to say:
It takes all the copper in your kitchen-in your rrfrigerator, range, washer, mixer, toaster-to make tne ammunition a -50 calibre machine gun fires in le s than a minute.
Thi- fantastic ratio of war to peace-one B-29 to 1,670 electric ranges, one tank to 47 refrigerators- is a problem that is straining every resource of the copper industry. Despite this enormous effort, it it imoos'ible to provide enough copper, brass and b-onze for our military needs and all our civil an wants as well.
The taxes on these things are regrettable but necessary. I think indirectly however this indicates a great rise in our standard of living when members here assert that it is the almost inalienable right of every young Canadian couple who get married to have an electric refrigerator, an electric washing machine and an electric stove. I do not think many members of this House of Commons started out in married life with those possessions.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would you like to go back
twenty-five years?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Now I come along to the sales tax. The minister, in his own presentation. brought it up by detailing expected revenues and showing that he was still $100 million short of meeting the extra defence expenditures which had been approved by this house, and therefore there was the remorseless necessity of increasing this basic sales tax. We did not change the base. That fact must be repeated. The sales tax today does not apply to food, fuel or building material. Each year we have widened that base. The minister put on the record the dominion bureau of statistics' estimate that only one-quar.er of the expenditures of a low income family are today subject to sales tax. But other members, such as the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) for example, traced the change in the sales tax over the years-the steadily mounting sales tax-and inferred that it was owing to government extravagance. Let me also point out other
The Budget-Mr. Sinclair things that have happened over the same years as the increase in the sales tax: Family allowances, $300 million; old age pensions, another $100 million; a national health program, $35 million. Those three items alone cost more than the $400 million which is raised today by the 8 per cent sales tax. I cannot help but think that the quotation from the minister on this point, as reported at page 1815, should be repeated in Hansard:
It is an inexorable rule of life that we can never really get something for nothing. Nothing is really free. Everything worth while has its costs. Tonight is the annual occasion when we count up the cost of our policies in terms of money. That cost is high, but failure to achieve our objectives of peace, security and financial integrity would involve infinitely greater and more painful cost.
The one suggestion that the hon. member for Greenwood had was that we could have avoided this increase in sales tax if the government would practise economy, if they would stop needless waste, extravagance and unnecessary expenditures. Early this session I made quite a long speech on this subject. The speech was prompted by the speech of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) out in Saskatoon, in which he said that he could save or lop off half a billion dollars from government spending, without affecting defence spending or necessary civilian services. In this house I repeated the challenge to him. I asked for the co-operation of every member of the house in indicating where the savings were to be made; because the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), as chairman of the treasury board, is more anxious than anyone else in this country to see such savings effected. Since that time I have been keeping a careful note here on my desk. Every time a Conservative member spoke, I listened for practical specific suggestions with respect to economy.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And you did not get any.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I did get one. I got almost one from the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and today the hon. member for Royal, who spoke before me, made the second practical suggestion. He said that from his own knowledge in his own riding he thought that perhaps, because of changed conditions, we could do without some of the lighthouses on the Saint John river. When I spoke earlier, that was the very thing that I invited hon. members to do. They have the best knowledge of conditions back in their ridings, as to what facilities are no longer necessary, and what facilities have superfluous staff. I sincerely thank the hon. member for bringing forward the only tangible and specific economy suggestion mentioned by the Tory party this session. It is true that members

The Budget-Mr. Sinclair of the opposition talk in resounding phrases about needless expenses for publications and travelling expenses. The hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Robertson) the other night pricked the bubble of this claim with regard to travelling expenses made by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming). The hon. member for Eglinton pointed out that despite these economies, travelling expenses are up $8 million; but the hon. member for Northumberland showed that they were up $8 million entirely because of added defence and defence production expenses and because the Royal Canadian Mounted Police had taken over another province, namely British Columbia. The Tories talk about publications and publicity generally, but never specifically. A little earlier this session I put through the Farm Improvement Loans Act, and two hon. members asked: How do farmers know about this. They do not seem to know enough. We should have more publicity. The hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Cardiff)-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am right here.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes; so I see. I said that we had not spent a great deal. He said, "You should be spending more on publicity." He is quite right and we are. When the Tories get down to specific instances, they find that the expenses are justified. So they content themselves with making these sweeping charges about extravagance, needless expenditures, Hoover commissions and halfbillion dollar savings. There is one place where they might get any information they please about any expenditure the government has made, audited by the controller of the treasury, audited by the Auditor General; that is in the public accounts committee. That takes hard work, of course. You cannot go in on a fishing expedition, as some of them do-open the book on public accounts and say, "What does this mean?" They should have had all the data that they could receive from the minister by way of orders for returns, from the department by way of letters, and from their constituents by way of knowledge of the services before they enter public accounts committee to ask about items. But let us see just what is the attendance of these economy-minded Conservatives on the public accounts committee. They have ten members on the committee headed by the leader of the opposition. In the meetings so far they have had in attendance three members, three members, six members, four members, four members, three members, two members; and never once has the leader of the opposition bothered to attend a meeting of the public accounts 

committee. He prefers of course to speak back in Saskatoon about half-billion dollar savings. He prefers to make these resounding speeches about extravagance and needless expenditures but never once to mention one specific economy. As I said when I spoke earlier, I was looking for suggestions for economy which these Conservatives were making and here I have three solid pages of notes which indicate that almost every member over there, some time since this session began has made, not suggestions for economy but rather many, many suggestions to increase government expenditures. I see that my friend the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) is in his place. I think he is the only personal friend I have in the Conservative party. He made a great speech in this house just a couple of days ago, and in it he did two things. In the first place, he decried government savings as far as the civil service was concerned; they were paltry, he said-5 per cent. Economy has to start somewhere.

I spoke of the post
office employees.
