speechtext:
Yes, he spoke of the post
office; that is quite true. Yet the post office is the biggest employer of labour in the government service. How are you going to make economies in the civil service if you do not do so in the post office which is the biggest employer? But while he wants to cut expenditure, and so save taxes, he says we are not doing enough in the Colombo plan and that, instead of spending $25 million, we should be spending $50 million. Fifty million dollars is one per cent on the present sales tax.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I did not
say that, as a matter of fact. My hon. friend apparently did not realize that I made no such statement the other day. Some weeks ago, in the course of a speech, I suggested that this was one expenditure that would be part of the defence expenditures of this country. I suggested $50 million. The government decided on $25 million. I raised no objection in any way the other day.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That is just my point. While that speech was on the radio, the speech the other day was almost the same, with the exception that in the one on the radio the hon. member advocated $50 million, but in the house just inferred it. Again desirable, I agree, but these are expenditures which do not decrease the tax rate of the Canadian people; they increase the tax rate of the Canadian people. The Liberal members of this house are willing to advocate such things, but they are also willing to have the necessary taxes to get these things. The

members of the C.C.F. also are very keen in advocating increased expenditures, but they do say the money can be found by soaking the corporations, or by running business themselves. Even the members of the Social Credit party have their solutions, and they tell us how money can be found. Only the Conservatives keep insisting on still greater expenditures in this house, but never suggest one means by which a specific saving can be made, except that the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) today suggested we could do away with certain lighthouses, and the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), speaking as the national chairman of the Progressive Conservative party, opposed the St. Lawrence seaway last week. We Liberals do think that the St. Lawrence seaway, which will cost us half a billion dollars, is a necessary and worth-while expenditure for all Canada. But it was nice to have on record the fact that the president of the national Progressive Conservative association, speaking in this House of Commons, opposes officially the St. Lawrence seaway. That is one economy on which the Tories have agreed.
I now want to make a few remarks on propaganda. In the old! days of parliamentary debate facts were countered by facts. It is true that some people shaded the facts, and some people quoted only the facts that suited them. But in the 1930's a new technique was developed by Joseph Goebbels, namely the technique of the big lie. Tell a big enough lie and tell it often, never quote facts, and in the end you will get perhaps the ignorant and the credulous to believe you. The Russians have picked it up. "Russia wants peace; Russia wants peace. The west wants war; the west wants war; the South Koreans and the United' Nations are the aggressors; the North Koreans are defending themselves". Repeat it endlessly and you may bring convictions. The one essential in this is to hammer away incessantly on the big lie, never support it by facts. Ignore facts, hoping to get the credulous, the ignorant and the misinformed to believe you. Today in Canada, the national Progressive Conservative party has adopted the technique of the big lie. They are barren of policy, devoid of an appeal to the Canadian people, unhappy in their leadership-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Nonsense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
-and so they have turned to this one great charge, "the government is extravagant; the government is wasting money; the government has needless expenditures"; but never do they come forward with tangible items saying: We will cut this out. Never do they restrain themselves from
The Budget-Mr. Sinclair making other demands on the treasury, they make endless bigger demands. I think the Canadian people are too well informed to fall, as did the Germans and as have the Russians, for the technique of the big lie. I think they have a great admiration for the great job, and the courageous job which has been done in connection with the finances of this country, both in war by the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley, and in the difficult days since the war by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott).
It would have been a very easy thing in these recent years, since the Minister of Finance has had surpluses, for him to have done one of two things: to have cut taxes across this country to make a good fellow of himself-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He did on the eve of an
election.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: -or, second, to have said yes to all those demands of the Conservatives for expenditures on Passamaquoddy and bigger subsidies on grain and hogs and cheese, and bonuses on gold, on floor prices for potatoes, on cheese and all the many things that they have advocated without ever mentioning the taxes to pay for them. Instead he chose to follow the path that any prudent Canadian, be he farmer, fisherman or businessman, has always followed. In good times, you pay off your debts. I think the most glowing tribute to the present Minister of Finance has not been said in glowing words in this debate but is found buried in the cold statistics of the public accounts. Page 50 of the public accounts shows the debt position of this country. Since 1867 to 1946 in only 15 years did we pay our way and have a surplus. The surplus in all those years totalled $300 million. Since the minister became Minister of Finance, in 1946 in the five budgets that he has presented every year we have had a surplus which has been applied to debt reduction. When he became Minister of Finance our net debt was $13,400 million. Today after reductions of five years of almost $2 billion-that means almost $60 million a year in interest charges saved- our net debt is $11,400 million. The people of Canada measure up that record of courage, that record of performance, against this Tory technique of the big lie, these continued, aimless charges of extravagance, waste and endless expenditures, and the position of the people of Canada today is the same as their position in June, 1949, when they gave such great endorsement to this government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, taking part in the budget debate one hesitates to take the time of this house

The Budget-Mr. Charlton to repeat many of the things said previously, but in some cases they bear repeating many times. The previous speaker has seen fit to repeat many of the things that the opposition have been saying on the matter for the last week. Whether his hindsight is better than his foresight remains to be seen. So far as the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) is concerned, I should like to tell him that if he would like to go back forty or fifty years, when he suggests that many hon. members did not have refrigerators and electric stoves when they started housekeeping, and for that reason probably the young couples today should not desire to have these things, I do not agree with him.
He also accused the party to which I have the honour to belong of the technique of the big lie. People in glass houses should not throw stones. The Progressive Conservative party at least say the same thing in the House of Commons as they do outside.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: George Valade!

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I wonder whether that can be said of many of the ministers of the crown in the past six months, because we have an instance of statements being made in the House of Commons when the education resolution was up for discussion some time ago, and the Liberal members all voted against that resolution, and one of the ministers saying outside that the government is prepared to give federal aid to education. Is that misrepresentation, or holding a carrot in front of the people on a stick?
Certainly the opposition is not the government. It is up to the government to bring forward a policy and to defend that policy. Certainly it cannot be said that the government has not all the powers necessary to control inflation; but what do they do? Next to nothing. "The time is not yet; not now, ater. Wait and see". The whole trouble is ipparently they have a wildcat by the tail and they can't let go. Neither are they trying ,o do anything to clip its claws.
In a radio speech last Tuesday evening, April 17, the Minister of Finance said that it was not price controls we need, but purse control. I consider it an insult to the Canadian people, Mr. Speaker, when the controller of their pocketbook tells them that they cannot spend money, but the governmen! continues merrily on its spending spree. From the best information available it would appear that we are facing a further increase in the cost of living, even before the budget was presented to this house.
It is no exaggeration to say that the tax increases announced by the Minister of Finance will materially contribute further

to existing difficult conditions, particularly on the lower income groups. In short, Mr. Speaker, it is no exaggeration to say that the actions of this government, as expressed through the Minister of Finance and the taxation measures he has selected, will certainly help the workingman in Canada to keep his head below water. It can have no other result. Certainly manufacturers are not going to absorb any portion of that extra tax, and as prices increase, taxes pyramid and the consumer pays. This has been proven in the case of cigarettes; the extra tax on cigarettes was three cents a package out the price increase was four cents. Gasoline and diesel oil are other examples of increases due directly to this budget. It is not common to see a man in work clothes smoking cigars, but the tax on cigars was not increased; it was increased only on pipe and cigarette tobaccos, products which the man in working clothes uses.
The special excise tax of 15 per cent for instance on stoves, refrigerators, washing machines and radios will make it that much more difficult for young couples starting up housekeeping. The tax on liquor was not increased. Most harsh of all, however, was the 25 per cent increase in the general sales tax, which will affect every citizen of this country. On June 4, 1940, the Hon. J. L. Ralston referred to the sales tax in these words:
We realize that increases in indirect taxes disguise the burdens imposed by the war, but they are much more likely to distribute these burdens harshly and unfairly.
And Mr. Ilsley on April 29, 1941, said this:
An increase in the sales tax has, I think, been fairly generally expected. At least there are evidences of a good deal of buying in anticipation of such an increase. This tax, while comparatively easy of administration and collection, and extremely productive, has marked defects as a fiscal instrument. After extended consideration we decided on balance against any increase. In coming to this decision we were not forgetful of the problems of agriculture, which would have been intensified had the sales tax been raised.
Later, on October 12, 1945, Mr. Ilsley made this comment concerning sales tax:
I have been impressed also with the extent to which the sales tax is having a discouraging effect on the rapid and efficient modernization of our productive equipment.
Later in the same speech he said this:
Particularly we should remove those taxes which imposed far back in the production process, increased costs out of proportion to the contribut-tion which they make to the revenue.
Surely, after all that the supporters of this government have said about the general sales tax, the government will now reconsider its position on this announced increase. Added to the highest cost of living ever recorded in

this country, these new tax impositions will cause almost unbearable distress on pensioners, and others in low income groups- those least able to bear added costs. Agricultural producers will be faced with higher costs at a time when production in certain commodities is already approaching a dangerously low level.
It has been said by many that food is too dear, and is the cause of the high cost of living. While food materially contributes to the cost of living, certainly the producer is getting only a very small percentage of the consumer dollar. The following is a short quotation from the Ontario Fruit and Vegetable Growers Association booklet, stating:
The urban public, with little knowledge of the agricultural processes, is always prone to blame the farmer for rising food prices. For some unknown reason the farmer should be content with small profits or small wages so the so-called consumer may have cheap food.
It is, therefore, interesting to break down the consumer dollar in an effort to ascertain who gets the most of it. Figures available on canned fruits and vegetables afford an excellent illustration.
The canned fruit or vegetable content per ton of raw product used varies with the efficiency and the equipment of each processor. The final yield is also affected by seasonal factors which increase or decrease the turnout, that is to say, the average quality of the produce, the percentage of waste, the high or low water content, etc. By and large, however, the following figures are average for the canning industry as a whole, based on 1950 contract prices to producers and present consumer prices at Ottawa stores:
Canned tomatoes: 28 oz. tin; yield 50 doz. tins per one ton of tomatoes, or 3J lbs. of tomatoes raw weight per tin. Consumer pays 18 to 20 cents: producer gets 3-5 cents per tin.
Tomato juice:	20 oz. tin; yield 100 doz. tins per
one ton of tomatoes, or 13 lbs. of tomatoes raw weight per tin. Consumer pays 11 to 12J cents; producer gets 1-8 cents per tin.
Sweet corn:	20 oz. tin or 14 oz. vacuum packed
tin (both contain approximately the same amount of product); yield 50 doz. tins per one ton of sweet corn, or 3J lbs. of sweet corn raw weight per tin. Consumer pays 141 to 18 cents. The producer gets 31 cents per tin.
Green peas: 20 oz. tin; yield 192 doz. tins per one ton of green peas, or l lbs. of green peas raw weight per tin. Consumer pays 15 to 21 cents; the producer gets 3-2 cents.
Green beans:	20 oz. tin; yields 200 doz. tins per
one ton of beans, or | lbs. of beans raw weight per tin. Consumer pays 14 to 27 cents; the producer gets 3-3 cents per tin.
Peaches:	20 oz. tin syrup pack-yield 1600 tins
per one ton of peaches, or 11 lbs. of peaches raw weight per tin. Consumer pays 25 to 28. Producer gets 5 7 cents per tin.
Variations in consumer prices depend on the grade-fancy, choice or standard. Further
The Budget-Mr. Charlton proof of this is found in figures taken from the United States Department of Agriculture, bureau of agricultural economics, appearing in the London Free Press of April 10, as follows:
Like this for example. Using last December's prices, if the farmer gave away the wool in a $50 suit of men's clothing the suit would still sell for $40.50. If he'd give away the wheat in a 16 cent loaf of bread the loaf would still cost the consumer 13-4 cents. If the farmer gave away the beans in a 16 cent can of pork and beans, the can would still cost you 14 cents at the grocery store. For cigarette smokers-
And these are American prices.
-if the tobacco grower gave away the tobacco in a 20-cent packet of cigarettes, the girl behind the counter would still ask you for 17 cents to pay for that purchase.
Net farm income has dropped appreciably in the last year. Nearly 100,000 farmers and farm workers have left farms over the last three years. Why? Because of the uncertainty of farm income. This government, through the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), has pernitted this condition to continue by failing to give leadership to agriculture. The penny-pinching policy of the Department of Agriculture, and failure to make adequate use of the Agricultural Prices Support Act, have cost the consumer of this country millions of dollars. All producers may not agree that the prices of food commodities may go too high. Butter did, because of the failure of the government to place the floor price high enough. Therefore production falls and prices increase.
The value of floor prices, if used wisely, is the steadying effect they have on production. It is a disadvantage to both producer and consumer to allow wide fluctuation in production, thence a comparable upward or downward movement of the consumer prices, depending on supply. Farmers cannot determine the year's output as can a factory owing to the dependence of the industry on the elements of nature. If the law of supply and demand were allowed to operate without some direction by producer organizations in co-operation with the government, it would inevitably follow that there would be low prices when supply exceeds demand, and high prices when the producer has little to sell. Price support could, in some degree, protect the producer when nature has been so kind. When production later proves insufficient to meet the demand, the reserve held in price support should then be released on the market. In this manner both producers and consumers gained something from the principle of price support. To support this statement I would like to quote from an

The Budget-Mr. Charlton article appearing in the Ottawa Journal of March 2, 1951:
Claims Price Floors for Producers Protected Consumers.
Without government price support, Canadians would be paying $1 a pound for butter and 80 or 90 cents a dozen for eggs, H. H. Hannam said today.
Support programs "have been of definite advantage to the consumer as well as the producer", the Canadian Federation of Agriculture president said in a speech before the annual meeting of the Ontario concentrated milk producers. Though price support programs for farm products have cost the government "a comparatively small amount", they have been of "definite advantage to the consumer as well as the producer." "If we had had no price support for butter and eggs, I am confident", said Mr. Hannam, "that the price by now might have been 80 or 90 cents a dozen for eggs and nearly a dollar for butter." Production would have dropped and products would have become scarce and prices of butter and eggs "would have been driven to the dollar mark."
The example of the last few months in the butter market should be sufficient proof that the floor price is too low. Cream producers of Canada through the dairy farmers of Canada and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture are of the opinion that it would require a floor price of 62 cents for butter to assure a reasonable supply for next winter and thus alleviate a repetition of the shortage and high consumer price of this year.
The whole dairy industry of this country is in a dangerous condition at the present time as explained so well by my colleague, the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair), earlier in this debate. Government policy has discouraged production. Government bulk trading contracts have not proved to be the Utopia the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) promised of them. I would like at this time to quote an editorial from .the Ottawa Journal of March 15, 1951:

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not discussing the wheat agreement at all; I am simply discussing bulk trading. The editorial continues:
It was an unsound method of selling wheat, with the result from the outset inevitable. As the Winnipeg Free Press puts it:
"Bulk sale contracts are unsound contracts. No buyer will enter into such contracts unless the price is lower than the market. That was true of the-"
I shall have to skip that.
"This is the lesson that the loss will not have been in vain if the producers learn that the only guarantee of selling their wheat for what it is worth is the market."
Since these bulk contracts did not prove as Utopian as the Minister of Agriculture had hoped, he now, in his characteristic fashion, tries to find a scapegoat. While addressing the Canadian Federation of Agriculture convention at Calgary, which I had the privilege of attending, the minister's whole speech was one of defence, and I quote from the Calgary Herald of January 23: British Pacts Could Be "Ridiculous"
J. G. Gardiner Outlines Canadian Trade Policy
"Every Liberal in the world believes that if we can maintain peace these agreements (British trade agreements with other countries) will very soon prove themselves to be the most ridiculous policies for promoting trade ever put into operation," Rt. Hon. James G. Gardiner, federal minister of agriculture told the Canadian Federation of Agriculture convention in the Palliser hotel this afternoon.

Defending government policy the minister referred to the history of commonwealth trading agreements to show that his government had opposed the idea of quota trading in 1936, but the Canadian government had already been committed by the Conservative government of Rt. Hon. R. B. Bennett.
His government had argued that such a plan was not suitable for a country such as Canada where agriculture could be expanded.
Until the second great war came the present government was not responsible for the plan but carried on "because no other plan was available." Canada had demonstrated that it could deliver greater quantities of food than it had been allowed under the British contracts but after the war other contracts with other countries were acknowledged.
The agricultural policies of the present federal government were actually those advocated by the government of Lord Bennett of Calgary when the latter was prime minister, Mr. Gardiner said in an interview.
In this all-out endeavour to extricate himself and his government the minister certainly had his wires crossed, as explained so well in the Winnipeg Free Press of February 10, a paper which by no stretch of the imagination could be said to be biased against the government. I quote:
Mr. Gardiner's Views
Speaking in this city a few days ago at the annual banquet of the Manitoba Liberal-Progressive Association. Mr. Gardiner, referring to bulk contracts remarked that he agrees with the views of the Free Press. "My friends of the Winnipeg Free Press" he said, "don't like bulk contracts. Neither do I. I have only one objection to the Winnipeg Free Press articles and that is they try to make you believe that I think differently to them on this subject." The only difference, he went on, was that he knew the history of this development and tried to place the blame where it belongs.
Mr. Gardiner's speech at Calgary on January 21 (the text of which is not to hand) explains his point of view in much more detail than his Winnipeg address. His argument is that the author of bulk trading, that is, government to government, or state buying and selling, was none other than Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. The Conservative party is the villain. The scene and occasion of the crime was the empire economic conference of 1932 where trade agreements with the United Kingdom were entered into by Canada, Australia, New Zealand and other members of the commonwealth.
Mr. Gardiner's argument is that he has been compelled, against his judgment, to engage in bulk trading because of two circumstances:
1.	The empire trade agreements of 19 years ago and,
2.	The British government will not trade in any other way.
On these grounds, Mr. Gardiner claims, he is compelled to do violence to the principles of trade which he regards as sound. There is, of course, no validity in Mr. Gardiner's first point. No bulk trading contracts were authorized by the empire treaties of 1932 and none were entered into by the Bennett government. Mr. Gardiner is confusing bulk contracts with quotas. What was done in 1932 was to adopt the principle of quotas-that is of restrictions upon total sales in the British market. Quotas and bulk contracts are as different as salt from sugar. Quotas are an extreme form of protection but, apart from this, do not interfere with private trade.
The Budget-Mr. Charlton
On the second count, Mr. Gardiner might reconsider his statement that bulk contracts are the only way in which the United Kingdom government will trade. Actually the United Kingdom has been buying all sorts of commodities other than wheat in large quantities. It has been buying lumber, copper, zinc, and many other items and in none of them has a bulk sale contract been regarded as essential. In all these purchases the British government has paid the market price-a point of great interest to Mr. Gardiner-thereby avoiding disagreeable claims by producers for compensation, such as are now being advanced with regard to the U.K.-Canada wheat agreement.
Producers were forced to take less than world prices by the government with the promise of assured future markets. Where are they? The cheese producers of Canada lost millions of dollars through government contracts. As a result of this, cheese production has been reduced to the lowest point in fifty years. Although cheese production is lower this year than last, we have never in Canada consumed all the cheese produced. What does the government propose to do with the surplus, however small it may be?
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make one suggestion to the Minister of Agriculture, and through him to the government, that I think would go far to (a) increase markets for the products of agriculture; (b) increase the quality of products now produced and thereby enhance the competitive position of Canadian agricultural products; (c) reduce production costs and bring to the original or primary producers a greater percentage of the ultimate consumer price.
I refer specifically to greater participation, made possible by government assistance and direction, in the field of chemurgic research. I read with interest what is being done in other countries and am alarmed at the slowness of Canada to participate in this work which has already proven so beneficial elsewhere. The Minister of Agriculture, in a speech in this house not long ago, referred to what had been done in the field of utilization of the soy bean in our economy. This is but one example of the tremendous advantages which can accrue to agriculture and the economy of this country by research in the fuller utilization of the products of the soil.
I would like at this point to draw to the attention of this house the possibilities in other fields, and I quote from the report of the National Chemurgic Council of America:
Filberts Flavour Cheese
American cheese of superior flavour can be produced with the aid of chemical agents obtained from filbert nuts.
Aside from its importance to the nation's cheese industry, this development is particularly ,good news for Oregon, where filberts are already a surplus crop and constantly increasing yields are promised by many young filbert orchards.

The Budget-Mr. Charlton
The filbert chemicals used in treating cheese are known as proteolytic enzymes, which means they are substances that help to digest proteins-in this case, milk proteins. They were tested for their effect on cheese flavour because of the present trend toward manufacture of American or Cheddar cheese from pasteurized milk, which produces milk cheese with less flavour and slightly different characteristics from those found in raw milk cheese.
Samples of Cheddar were taken out of a commercial cheese vat after milling and salt was added. A measured volume of the filbert extract was added to each experimental sample and a similar volume of water to the control samples.
The regular processing and storage procedures were then carried out, all the samples being checked at regular monthly intervals.
At the end of four months, expert cheese tasters pronounced the cheese made with the filbert extracts to have much better flavour than all the other samples, including the controls. It was better aged. The control samples had a mild clean flavour which did not compare with the superior flavour of the treated samples. In addition to this improvement in flavour, the ripening time was substantially shortened, which is of economic importance because of the expense for storage rooms. It should be emphasized that no filbert nut flavour was transferred to the treated cheese by the filbert extracts.
Proteolytic enzymes have been isolated from many plants. The presence of a protein-digesting substance in the leaves and green fruit of the papaya tree (carica papaya) has long been known. The existence of a similar meat-digesting enzyme in the juice of the pineapple was first noted in 1891 by a Venezuelan scientist named Marcano. Figs, milkweed, lima beans, and the kernels of wheat also have been found to contain such enzymes. The work on filberts was prompted by a search for new uses for Oregon's surplus nuts.
As I stated before, the farmers are discouraged. With mounting costs and continued scarcity of farm labour many farmers are changing their programs to conform to the shorter work week in industry. This, however, is impossible for the dairy farmer, hence many are quitting that branch of the industry. The Canadian Weekly Newspapers Association has recognized the agricultural problem, and I quote from an article appearing in the Globe and Mail of March 9, 1951:
Rural Canada Hit Hard by Wage-Raising Trend, Weekly Papers Warn
Ottawa, March 9-A dangerous unbalance exists between the rural and urban economies of Canada, Prime Minister St. Laurent and members of his cabinet were warned today in a brief presented by the Canadian Weekly Newspapers Association. The brief, presented by W. E. McCartney, managing director, pointed specifically to the recent trend toward raising wages, curbing productive hours of work, and said that this placed an unfair economic burden on rural Canada.
The consequence of this trend is that milk production is down half a billion pounds in the last three years. The cow population has been reduced by almost a half million since 1945, while our human population has increased by one and three-quarter million in the same period. If this trend is allowed

to continue, and certainly there has been no apparent move by the government to stop it, then production will continue to decline. Either the dairy industry must be placed on a profitable basis or supplies will be short with resultant high prices. Consumers are beginning to tell their children now that the beef steer, not the cow, is jumping over the moon. This is not a healthy situation for either the producer or the consumer, and I am sure the dairy farmers of Canada do not want extremely high prices. On the other hand if the government does not take some remedial action the dairy cow could quite conceivably be replaced by products made from cheap imported vegetable oils. A low price for a farm product is no advantage to consumers. They have to make up for it later on when supply drops off. The best example of this fact was the terrific increase in egg prices last year, following the refusal for two months by this government to place a floor price under eggs when the bottom dropped out in December 1949, and hundreds of flocks were sold off.
I should like to quote from a Canadian Press article appearing in the Globe and Mail of March 1, 1951:
Food Producers Merit Fair Prices, Gardiner Holds
Ste. Anne de Bellevue, Quebec, Feb. 27-Canadian Press-Agriculture Minister Gardiner said today that Canadian food producers have two primary objectives-to produce enough food for our own people and to sell at a sufficiently high price to encourage them to keep on producing.
New Zealand butter, which Mr. Gardiner said the government did not want to see brought into Canada, was laid down at Halifax at a cost of 40-4 cents a pound. The floor price in Canada was 53 cents. Canadian farmers could not compete with New Zealand butter. The butter dealers were selling the imported butter at 56] cents a pound.
"The market price in this country must be comparatively high," said the minister.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) stated that the four and a half million pounds of New Zealand butter was laid down at Halifax for 40 [DOT] 4 cents per pound and sold for 56J, resulting in a profit of at least a million dollars which the government should have had in view of the maintained floor price of 53 cents. The government in effect subsidized a good share of that very juicy profit. In cases where a floor price is being maintained on any product and a short position is encountered, then the government itself, under such conditions, should import a sufli-cient quantity to satisfy the conditions, should import a sufficient quantity to satisfy the domestic demand. What did this government do? They closed the door on January 24 by order in council, placing butter imports under government control; but somebody had his foot in the door, because on January 27 it was

opened again by the cancellation of the order in council. No reason was given or explanation offered; just cancelled.
In the event of a war, the food situation in Canada could be serious. In the case of most field crops, dependent on the weather of course, production could be stepped up in a year with sufficient help. The same would be true of poultry and hogs.
Dairy products, beef and sheep, however, would take nearly three years, even with the most stringent controls. I would urge the government, therefore, to make the necessary use of the Agricultural Prices Support Act. Incorporate within the act some formula upon which to base the floor price, thereby relieving the constant fear in the minds of the producers of our nation's food, and assure the production of at least our own domestic requirements.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after such a friendly reception perhaps I should, in reciprocation, make my speech short so the members can get away before six o'clock. In my brief observation of events here. Mr. Speaker. I have noticed a disposition to invoke the blessing of the deity, and to call on powers other than those conferred by membership in this house. I may say that at this point I am in entire sympathy and accord with the feelings which prompt such utterances. Someone wiser than I once said that there is nothing new under the sun. I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that thought must have occurred many times in the minds of hon. members as another new member launched forth on his maiden speech. This is particularly true in my case because Halifax constituency has been so ably represented by my predecessor, the Hon. Senator Isnor, and by the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey), so I can add very little to what has been said before.
In the light of the present fast moving events it might be well to remind you that Halifax city, which is the centre of our constituency, was founded 202 years ago as a military outpost. No doubt there are some people who are unkind enough to suggest it is still an outpost of Toronto, perhaps, or Saint John. But had Halifax, the warden of the honour of the north, not been pioneered first, even the constituency of Springfield might still be a wilderness.
The riding is large in size, and has a population of roughly 150,000. Most, of the people live along the coast line, for the sea is very important to their livelihood. It is a .
The Budget-Mr. Balcom heavily forested area which supports a substantial lumber industry, and there is some farm land. Over 75 per cent of the population is concentrated in the Halifax-Dartmouth area bordering on the magnificent harbour which is the heart of the community. Despite the growth in industry, commerce, business and educational services, Halifax is never far removed psychologically from the feature that prompted its origin, namely the strategic value of its harbour. This port is, unfortunately, apt to be forgotten by the rest of Canada between wars, not intentionally but because we are far away from the more populous areas.
I need not remind you of its part in world wars I and II, and even as far back as the Riel rebellion and the South African war in 1899-1902, when Halifax sent a regiment of its own. I hardly need to assure you that it is ready to play its part again in strengthening our defences against aggression or, if the worst should come, active participation in the war for our way of life.
At this point, perhaps I should mention a misunderstanding that arose in connection with a statement attributed to our minister of health and welfare, the Hon. Harold Connolly. When speaking in Florida, he was misquoted by the newspapers.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: That is always the case when they say the wrong thing.

He gave a denial to the
Halifax Chronicle-Herald of April 21, stating that he had made no mention of union between Canada and the United States. The article reads in part:
Anything might happen at any time, I said. Who could tell? As to the "affinity" matter, we were talking on the socialist government in Britain as compared with the democratic government in Canada. On this point I expressed the view that socialism would never take over the government in Canada and that in this connection Canada and the United States had much in common, both peoples preferring to live under a system of democracy.
I am sure most members in this house will agree with what Mr. Connolly has said in his denial, including the member for Royal (Mr. Brooks).

speechtext:
Coming back to the strategic importance of the riding, the heavy concentration of naval and military establishments there creates serious problems in civic government. Tax-exempt property representing 50 per cent of our total assessment has to be serviced and protected as well as civilian establishments. The existence of such in any

The Budget-Mr. Balcom community is a problem. Add to that a personnel establishment that increases and contracts from time to time, and you have a heavy burden on city services.
The federal government has recognized its responsibilities in this regard by some payments already made in lieu of taxation of crown property. I note with satisfaction that measures will be considered during this session respecting federal grants to municipalities. The special position of Halifax and Dartmouth must be recognized and an equitable arrangement made regarding these obligations.
The burden of the speech from the throne and indeed most of the proceedings of the house to date have left little room for any but the most sober appraisal of our responsibilities here. The forthright account of events in the international field given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) has shown the gravity of the situation confronting us. The part Canada will play in the drive for collective defence has been outlined. The magnitude of the commitments has been well described as "staggering".
'The means of financing these commitments are rather painful and there has been heated debate on some aspects of government policy to that end. Nevertheless, I believe that the reaction to the budget bears out what the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said in presenting it, as reported at page 1798 of Hansard:
. . . there are no great issues of principle dividing us ... on the major questions of policy underlying my proposals we are all fundamentally agreed.
It is apparent that for many years we shall have to turn our energy from the constructive pursuits which we should like to follow. Our productive capacity must be devoted to an increasing degree to defence instead of primarily to improving the standard of living of our people. The need for physical defence is paramount but in our haste to this end we must be careful not to neglect other values fundamental to our well-being.
We have been informed that we may expect the report of the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences during this session. In Canada we have some peculiar problems in the field of culture and education, and the findings of this commission are awaited with much interest. The field is of the utmost concern; for, apart from its intrinsic importance, the heaviest strain of the next few years will fall upon our mental and spiritual resources. It is well known that the upheaval of war subjects the average individual to the lure of the "eat, drink and be merry" philosophy. It is equally

so of a nation. In our preoccupation with defence let us not neglect the values which make our sacrifices worth while.
There may be some thought during this difficult period in the world's history that we should concentrate all our energies in holding back the flood of aggression. That is all very fine in itself, but it is not my view. The world conflict cannot be solved by setting aside the very elements that have made our civilization strong. Democracies must never stand still.
But even under the threat of war we must go forward with every plan to improve our way of life. For this reason I commend the undertaking of the government to provide pensions for those 70 and over without the means test; pensions for the needy between 65-70; and possibly aids to the handicapped. Of particular importance are the grants to our universities and I would stress those grants to our schools of social work which are contributing so much to the welfare of our people. I have hope that ample allowance has been made for these schools of social work in the estimates of the Department of National Health and Welfare. In terms of our total expenditures on welfare payments to individuals, an investment in training facilities is a moderate cost to ensure that these payments are well spent. The minister has always been generous in the provision of such assistance, and he is well aware of their contribution and of the desirability, or even the need, to have them function independently of the government.
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, that more people were unable to see the picture which was shown the other night in this building, when the work of the social worker was screened. The scenes were in British Columbia, but we might say that the picture that was shown there would be typical of all the provinces. British Columbia people should be proud that their province was chosen for the scenes.
Our Canadian pattern is made strong by all thp complex forces involved in it. The active part played in our social life by voluntary groups cannot be overestimated, and we should be very thankful that these voluntary groups are so eager to work.
I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the world conflict today is between truth and confusion. We must not fail our conviction that we are on the right road to progress, that the ordinary men and women of this earth can find, in company with us, the right way to the future. We should maintain and strengthen all voluntary activities in Canada that serve to enrich Canadian life. Communism with all its vain promises

and all its sordid performances cannot be answered by words alone.
Those of us fortunate enough to live in Nova Scotia want to say that we are ready at all times to stand with the rest of Canada and bear our share in times of stress. The right hand of the Dominion of Canada that reaches far out into the Atlantic ocean, we have borne the brunt of wars since 1605, in the days of de Monts and Champlain, and in Halifax since the arrival of Lord Cornwallis in 1749. But the fact of our being on the fringe of such a far-flung country and the fact of our being connected with the rest of Canada by a railway, the location of which was determined primarily by strategic considerations, have created some difficulties. Various measures have been implemented to mitigate the economic handicaps resulting from transportation costs, but many problems remain. The royal commission on transportation has taken cognizance of these matters peculiar to the various regions in Canada. We in the maritimes are particularly gratified that the report recognizes the validity of our objections to horizontal freight rate increases.
On another recommendation of this same report, there is not so general approval. I refer to the formation of a local advisory committee for our Halifax harbours board. Had we had such an advisory committee operating at this time, the unfortunate accidents which have occurred recently might have been avoided. We are still convinced that remote control is not in the best interests of our national harbours.
Normally, Halifax is a winter port, partially used during the winter, only slightly used during the summer when the St. Lawrence river is open, but totally used in an all-out war. Halifax harbour has untold advantages over any other Atlantic port-with commiseration to Saint John-as we have very little tide, no great windstorms; suitable docks, with more under construction; excellent anchorage; and "fair" railway services. I say "fair" because I consider that the Canadian Pacific Railway should be running over its own rails into Halifax or at least have running rights over the C.N.R. In no way is this a reflection on the excellent service given by the Canadian National Railways but the lack of competition is hurting not only Halifax but all of Nova Scotia.
The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne) in the house last week drew attention to the rail and water services between the mainland and Newfoundland, and he stated that he had suggested to the president of the Canadian National Railways the desirability of operating steamships between
The Budget-Mr. Balcom Halifax or Montreal and St. John's. Since almost 40 per cent of the people of Newfoundland are in the Avalon peninsula, a great deal of the traffic to the island should be brought to St. John's by water from Halifax.
When Newfoundland entered confederation, it was arranged that the Canadian National Railways regard the boat haul from Sydney to Port aux Basques as a railway route. Although the merchandise has to be transshipped several times, rates are set on the basis that it is an all-rail route. This has meant the diversion of traffic which would logically go to St. John's via Halifax.
Merchandise, particularly heavy equipment, furniture, and the like, when it is routed in such a way that it has to be unloaded and reloaded several times, really calls for export packaging which is very costly. Freight for St. John's landed at Port aux Basques has to be carried 550 miles across the island over a railroad already busy serving its own area.
It is reported that the loss to the Canadian National Railways on Newfoundland operations during 1950 amounted to $3 million, exclusive of a subsidy of $1,250,000 on the coastal steamship operations. I would respectfully suggest that if the freight intended for St. John's and the Avalon peninsula were directed through Halifax, this deficit would be greatly reduced. This would not interfere with the freight which would, by reason of its destination, naturally be shipped through North Sydney. The fastest, the best, and the route that calls for the least handling of freight should be the one adopted and in respect to goods going to the Avalon peninsula, Halifax is the logical shipping point. I appreciate the efforts of the hon. member for St. John's West in advocating some such arrangements.
As you know, Halifax is not only a shipping port, but is also the home port of a considerable fishing fleet which sails to the nearby fishing banks, most prolific and least depleted in the world. The port has, too, a considerable stake in the inshore fisheries. A large proportion of the rural population who live along the coast line are dependent on the fishing industry for a whole or a part at least, of their livelihood. I am, therefore, keenly interested in anything that affects that group of people.
The announcement in the budget regarding certain tariff changes affecting fishermen's supplies will be good news to our constituents. The free entry of diesel engines used in commercial fishing operations and widening of the provision covering nets

Mr. Speaker, I rise to say a few words in the budget debate. The hon. member who immediately preceded me voiced his opinion of the manner in which the government has been carrying on the affairs of the people. I am sure everything he said met with the unanimous approval of one hundred per cent of government front and back benches.
The hon. member made the further statement that Sir John A. Macdonald had said that a government with a large majority was not always the best thing for a country. Sir John A. Macdonald made very few mistakes, and in that assertion he was absolutely right.

What have we heard from the government with regard to old age pensions? I am not talking about pensions for the man who says that because he has reached the age of seventy, eighty or ninety years he is entitled to a pension. I am talking about the man or woman who cannot exist without a pension or a subsidy from the taxpayers. I am not talking about the man who is willing and able to work; I refer to those needy people of seventy years and over. What about the $40 on which they are barely existing? I venture to say some of them are not
[Mr. Sinnott.l

existing at all; they still have to look to charitable institutions and neighbours in order to exist-and that in this land of plenty!
What about the crippled people in Canada? We have been sitting here since the latter part of January, and I would ask what the government has done to help bedridden people. There are bedridden people who have been crippled for life who cannot provide for themselves. That is a blotch on the reputation of this government, yet we have the unanimous desk-thumping of the Liberal members. What about our shortages?
Where is the vision of the people who built this country? Can similar vision be found among the ministers of this government? What about the steel situation? We are selling now steel by the ton to the United States for $5 and buying it back at $100 per ton finished. What about the nail situation? Every time nails are mentioned there are laughs from the members of the Liberal party. But it is no laughing matter for a man who wants a roof over his head for himself, his wife and children. What about the cement situation? Has this government gone to the manufacturers of steel and told them that if they do not expand their plants, the government will?
I am a free enterpriser from the word go, but if I was a member of any government which did not lay down the law to the steel companies of Canada, which had not taken this action five, six or seven years ago, I would soon quit that party.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Go back to cement.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

This applies to cement as well. Keep the government out of business as long as you possibly can, but when you cannot avoid it get into business. First of all, any government represents the people. If private enterprise cannot cope with the situation, the government has the facilities to do so. I know that members of the Liberal party agree with my assertions. They know it is all too true.
In this modern day and age you cannot ask people to go into a home in the city or country without a hot water boiler to heat water for the children, for washing, for dishes, for clothes and so on. What do we find? When after great struggles a man gets a roof on, gets the doors on, probably gets a furnace in, he is faced with the fact that there are no hot water boilers available in this great banner province of Ontario in the Dominion of Canada. In resuming my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief; but in dealing with the last item I wish to discuss I think I will be able to point out clearly, if not to the members of the government at least to the people of Canada, that by its handling of this one matter the government has proven beyond peradventure that it has utter disregard for the value of the money that comes from the taxpayers, and that it is not carrying out the trust the citizens of Canada .placed in it when the government was elected to power in 1949.
Everyone in Canada, irrespective of party, is in favour of a home for the Prime Minister. Everyone wants a home that will be in keeping with the position. The duties of the Prime Minister and those of the Governor General are entirely different; there is no doubt about that. The Prime Minister is one of the busiest men in Canada; but at no time has the Prime Minister of this or any other country been called upon to perform the

The Budget-Mr. Ferguson duties or functions of the Governor General. Yet we find the taxpayers of Canada, having no more to say about it than simply voting this government into power, called upon to pay a bill which I estimate will amount to something like $800,000. When it is completed I think it will be found that I am not far wrong; probably I will be $100,000 short.
When this residence was conceived, considered and finally begun by this government, apparently no definite over-all price was fixed, taking into consideration the high costs of construction, furnishings, maintenance and so on. I contend that if the government could be so far out in interpreting the feelings of the Canadian people with respect to the edifice in the course of construction, to be known as the Prime Minister's home, they might well be out and are out on almost everything they have tackled on behalf of the people of this country. Most of us, through curiosity or of necessity, have passed the building which is to be occupied by the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and those following him. None of us is so childish as not to know something about the cost of construction. That building today represents an expenditure of more than half a million dollars. We know something of what might be expected from the expenditure of a quarter of a million dollars on a residence. If the completed building is in keeping with the amount already spent it is going to cost the taxpayers tremendous amounts to keep it in repair and to maintain the furnishings. The government is constantly talking about cutting expenditures, but makes no effort to do so. I do not like to bring up this matter of the Prime Minister's home, but it is something which is of interest to the whole country. It is something of which Canadians should be proud, but one can hardly be proud of anything so costly that it means our pocketbooks will be pinched in order to pay for it. Every member of this house must realize that there is not a more blatant, brazen case of flagrant squandering of public funds than has occurred in connection with this building.
I do not want to be mean about it. Never let it be said that Julian Ferguson did not want a home for the Prime Minister in keeping with the dignity of that position, but there is a great difference between a home in keeping with that position and a home the taxpayers cannot afford, and that is what we have today. Compare it with 10

Downing street, which has housed some of the greatest men the world has ever known, where in the past some of the greatest national ideas and ideals have been conceived, which has been occupied by some of the greatest brains the British empire has ever seen. I shall do so from now on. I was addressing the hon. member because I was carried away for the moment.
I am afraid that in our efforts to effect a curb on prices up to now, we are perhaps

The Budget-Mr. Riley overlooking those citizens who are beginning to class themselves as being in the forgotten estate. The imposition of price and wage controls at the present time would leave them as helpless as they are now because their present wages are hopelessly inadequate. This may sound like an exaggeration, but I would defy anybody, as the head of a family of three or four, with small children, and living in a city, in rented accommodation, to feed, clothe and house that family today on an income of $125 or even $150 a month. It just cannot be done. Because those whom I describe find it virtually impossible to move about in quest of more lucrative employment, some agency should be established by the government or otherwise whose duties it would be to assist these people to obtain a more equitable return for their services.
The last time I had the privilege of speaking in this chamber I expressed some considerable concern over the unemployment figures in my own constituency and in other maritime constituencies. Since then I have seen very real evidence of the effort which is being made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) to direct, wherever reasonable and feasible, a flow of defence work to industries in our eastern provinces. His appointment of responsible officers in his new Department of Defence Production to ensure continuity of this policy is being received with a sense of relief by our people.
I am also pleased at the interest which is being shown in providing work for the large drydock and shipbuilding yards in my own city of Saint John, where both management and employees as well as citizens generally are eagerly awaiting news of an extensive program of construction and repairs. I would imagine that perhaps this policy will even be enlarged upon after the Minister of Trade and Commerce reads the speech which was so ably delivered by my friend the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson). Up until now work has not been sufficiently steady in this industry to warrant our steel workers remaining in Saint John, and we have been in constant danger of losing them to other and busier yards.
I would call the attention of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) to the necessity for extending dock facilities on the eastern side of Saint John harbour. Since the completion of the Pugsley terminal a little more than a year ago, we have been left with excellent docking and loading facilities which cannot be properly exploited unless this new pier is extended at least to Reed's Point, so-called, which lies directly south of it. The recently-experienced congestion on the


western side of our harbour has brought sharply into focus the necessity for completing this project. Until this extension is proceeded with, it will not be possible to lay railway tracks between the large new sheds and the face of the pier and thus make it possible to load lumber and other cargoes aboard ship without loss of money, time and effort.
Saint John harbour is one of the most important shipping points in this country, and I say that with due and humble apologies to the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Balcom). As the present crisis develops, it becomes increasingly urgent that we make every possible effort to meet an emergency. When the broad general curbs were put on the expenditure of public funds for all but essential public projects, surely these curbs were never intended to apply to a pier for ocean-going vessels which is just as essential to our defence requirements as are jet fighters or field artillery. If the construction of this pier is not proceeded with at the present time, we may shortly be facing congestion of a most serious nature brought on by an emergency which hovers on the horizon. When the supplementary estimates are brought down, I sincerely hope that provision will be made therein for completion of this vital project.
I shall hold until a later date my appraisal of the report of the Turgeon commission on transportation, but references made to the seaway project in the course of this debate impel me to say that the finding of that commission in respect of the Chignecto canal leaves me with a cold feeling toward the St. Lawrence seaway. Like the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Richard), I am not opposed to this project; but it is difficult for us to become enthusiastic over it when the Turgeon commission, after but a cursory examination of only a small part of the evidence available, and that of a documentary nature, has so effectively shut the door on the arguments put forward in support of the Chignecto canal. That part of the report dealing with the canal has as effectively stunned a large section of our population in the Atlantic provinces as though they had been sandbagged.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tonight I should like to deal with three aspects of the current budget. The first aspect with which I should like to take issue is the fact that there is no increase in the tax on alcoholic spirits, while at the same time the taxes on many of the necessities of life have been materially increased.
If there ever was a luxury, it is alcoholic spirits; and those who consume them can certainly afford to pay an increased tax. If

the tax had been increased on alcoholic spirits, it would have been possible to eliminate, or greatly to reduce, the increased tax which has been imposed on many of the necessities of life.
In this action I believe that the government is guilty of favouring those who can afford luxuries, at the expense of those who are struggling, against an ever-increasing cost of living, to feed, clothe and house their families.
The second aspect of this budget with which I should like to take issue is the fact that it contains no provision for halting the ever-increasing rise in prices. The increased taxes themselves add to the cost of living. Unless price control is immediately imposed, prices will continue to rise, and pensioners and others in the lower income groups will continue to suffer ever-increasing hardship and privation.
I believe that this persistent refusal on the part of the government to bring in price control is a callous disregard of the needs of the people.
The third aspect of this budget with which I should like to take issue is the statement made recently by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that those serving in our armed forces overseas are no longer exempt from the income tax.
This is a complete reversal of the policy adopted by the present government during the last war; a policy which met with widespread and general approval by all of the people of this country.
In attempting to explain his action, the minister said he believed that no type of employment in this country should be exempt from income tax. That is quite satisfactory when applied to those of us who live and work in the comfort and security of Canada, but it is quite another matter when you are dealing with men who are daily risking their lives to fight our battles overseas.
I believe that those who serve overseas in our armed forces should be exempt from income tax. That is the very least we' can do for these gallant men.
Now I should like to deal with a matter which is of vital importance to all Canadians, namely, the matter of a health insurance plan for this country.
One of the great needs of people today is to find some way by which the financial cost of sickness or accident can cease to impose a crippling burden of debt upon .individuals and families.
When sickness or accident strikes today, one of two things usually happens; either the 80709-1474
The Budget-Mr. Hees proper care and treatment are not given, because the financial cost is too high; or, if proper care and treatment are given, the family or the individual is dealt a financial blow, from which it may take many years to recover.
I believe that we cannot allow either of those conditions to continue any longer. Both can be overcome by a system of universal contributory health insurance.
It is obvious that if a health insurance plan is to be successful, it must receive the wholehearted support and co-operation of the doctors and dentists of this country. It must interfere as little as possible with the present method of administering to the health of this country, which has proved to be very satisfactory indeed. It should concern itself with finding some better method by which people can pay their bills for the medical and dental services which they do receive. Now, how can this best be done?
I believe that the system employed in Great Britain today is not satisfactory, because it has succeeded in lowering the quality of service to the individual. All services in Great Britain have been free, and the "something-for-nothing" aspect has caused those who really do not need treatment to flock to the doctor's office. They have done so in such large numbers that the time which the doctor or dentist can devote to any individual patient is so short that the treatment which any one patient can receive is, of necessity, superficial.
The "something-for-nothing" aspect of the British plan is, of course, a complete myth, because the full cost of the plan must be borne by the people, both in regular contributions and in taxes.
I believe that the best kind of plan for this country is that which has proved successful in Sweden and in a number of other European countries for a number of years. Under that plan, 75 per cent of the cost of treatment or hospitalization is met out of a health insurance fund, which is maintained by regular contributions from all of the people.
The other 25 per cent of the cost of treatment or hospitalization is paid by the patient, and this removes the "something-for-nothing" aspect of the British plan. It is sufficient to ensure that those applying for treatment really do need it. On the other hand, it is not so much as to impose a severe financial burden on the individual or on the family.
It is obvious, I believe, that the 25 per cent of the bill which the patient pays reduces the over-all cost of the plan by that amount, and the regular monthly contributions which the people pay are therefore 25 per cent less

The Budget-Mr. Wright than they would be under a plan which pays for the whole cost of the treatment. The cost of the plan is also kept to a minimum, because only those who really need treatment apply for it.
The scale of fees which doctors and dentists would charge could be set up very easily through consultation with the medical and dental professions. The doctor-patient relationship will remain exactly the same as it is today. The only change would be that the patient would pay 25 per cent of the bill, and the doctor would submit his account for the remaining 75 per cent to the health insurance fund.
I believe that this type of plan will work, and that it will materially improve the health of the people by insuring that they receive the proper treatment when they need it, without imposing an undue financial burden either upon the individual or upon the family.
I believe that this type of plan should be studied by the government, and should be presented to parliament for its consideration at the very earliest opportunity.

He quoted from this publication to prove certain points with which I shall deal later. Before he did that however he indicated that some people, in making statements and speeches, are apt to shade the facts. He used that argument in an effort to justify certain publications put out by the government to make the people better acquainted with the facts.
But sometimes, even in publishing facts, such facts can be stated on one side of a case, and shaded to an even greater extent than if no statement had been made at all. I do not think the hon. member should have used the expression "shading the facts", when he was criticizing recommendations from this side of the house with regard to higher income tax. As a matter of fact the hon. member for Coast-Capilano gave the impression that the wealthier people in this country were retaining only $4 out of every $100 subject to income tax. He did not say, however, that the man who is receiving an income of $250,000 has over $50,000 left after he has paid his income tax. He did not say that there is kept out of his income $96 out of each $100 only when the income exceeds a quarter of a million dollars. In other words he still keeps $4,000 out of every $100,000 over the quarter of a million dollars of income; and I am sure he is not being hurt at all by that procedure. He still has a very good income remaining, and is in a much better position than the old age pensioner, those who are receiving widows' allowances and many other persons on fixed incomes in this country.
I think the hon. member for Coast-Capilano was perhaps shading the facts a bit when he quoted only one small portion from the pamphlet to which I have referred and which has been issued and distributed. It seems to me there are many interesting facts set out, and I should like to place on the record tonight some that the hon. member failed to place on the record this afternoon. He took only that part which suited his own argument.
The pamphlet is entitled "This Cost of Living Business," and covers widely the position in Great Britain in connection with the cost of living in and the productivity of that country. The hon. member for Coast-Capilano suggested that if those of us in this group were placed in a position where we had to bring down a budget we would tax corporations to a point where they would

have nothing left for reinvestment, and there would be no capital expansion in the country.
I would bring to the attention of the house the fact that this party was organized in 1932, at a time when there was very little capital expansion, at a time when, because of the failure of private enterprise to make the necessary capital expansion and to develop the resources of the country, hundreds of thousands of people were without employment. One of the objectives of this group was to see that we stopped this boom and bust economy we have under free enterprise, so that we might have in Canada an expansion of our productivity which would give employment to all our people and would develop the resources of the country as they should be developed.
The government in Great Britain has increased the productivity of that country. In this pamphlet it states that productivity is increasing rapidly.

speechtext:
The cost of living in Canada went up 4 [DOT] 5 points in one month and undoubtedly will show a rise in the future when the results of this budget are incorporated in retail prices. There is no doubt that some of the features in the budget will act against inflation in their long-term effect, but the short-term effect of the budget will be to create further inflation. You cannot increase the sales tax by 25 per cent, a tax which is imposed on a large proportion of the goods consumed in this country, without an inflationary effect. You cannot increase the excise taxes on other goods without the first effect being inflationary.
Some parts of the budget, such as that part wherein they have taken steps to prevent depreciation being allowed on certain types of construction for the next four years, no

doubt in its long-term effect will be deflationary. As a matter of fact that is something which we in this group have been trying to bring to the attention of the government for some time. The accelerated depreciation allowed to industry by this government immediately after the war was inflationary. One of the major causes of the present inflation in this country was the tremendous amount of money spent on capital expansion. While a reasonable amount of capital expansion is absolutely necessary, it is possible to have too much especially for the production of non-essential goods.
This article shows that there is being used for capital expansion in Great Britain about 20 per cent of the total production. According to the figures given by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), if my memory serves me correctly, we are spending about 18 per cent of our total production in capital expansion. Only when we balance our capital expansion against the sale of goods will we have a balanced economy. There will have to be some planning of our economy if we are not to have the booms and-busts we had in the past.
Because of certain measures introduced by the government immediately after the war in their decontrol policy and in giving accelerated depreciation on capital expansion we have the inflationary spiral in which we find ourselves today. That was one of the major causes. While I admit that certain parts of the budget are deflationary in effect, nevertheless the immediate effect is inflationary. I do not think that anyone who considers the budget as a whole can get away from the fact that it is inflationary.
As far as we in this group are concerned, we have always believed that we should set aside a certain amount of our national income each year for capital expansion. That is one of the first principles of this party. We agree that you cannot have your pie and eat it too. If the hon. member for Ottawa West would get a copy of Comment for March, 1951, published by the C.C.F., he would be able to get some idea of the policy of this group with regard to capital expansion. With regard to the slice of the Canadian pie, which is the total productivity of this country, it has this to say:
The size of your particular piece will depend on these and other factors:
(1)	The size of the pie itself.
(2)	The proportion devoted to investment in capital goods.
And later on:
The bigger the pie the more there is likely to be for each. Thus, we all have a stake in higher production. To get maximum production we must employ all our human and material resources. Nobody should be out of work and no factories

should be idle. To make the biggest possible pie we must have the highest possible rate of productivity. This means both a full day's intelligent work each day by the members of the labour force and the best possible tools and equipment for the labour force to work with.
With regard to the reinvestment of capital, it states this:
Capital investment should be stabilized at an appropriate proportion so that we shall have continually increasing productivity in the years ahead. (The proportion was 18 per cent in 1950). It would be foolhardy to seek a bigger piece of pie this year if it means smaller ones in the years ahead.
It is essential that there be capital investment in any country. The basic policy of this group is that that capital investment should be planned so that there will be capital investment in new production and the bringing in of new resources over the years. That portion of the profits of corporations which is put back into capital investment for the production of necessary goods would never be touched by this party. It is absolutely essential that there be reinvestment in capital production. One of the things that we object to is a corporation coming into this country, investing in our natural resources, and then taking the profits which they make out of this country rather than reinvesting them in Canada. That is one type of profit which we believe should be taxed. The reinvestment of capital for the purpose of expanding production and developing our resources has always been a major plank in the platform of this group. Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Ottawa West got me away from the matter I was discussing, but perhaps that is a good thing if it has removed any doubt from his mind as to the policies of this group with respect to capital investment.
Before concluding I should like to deal briefly with the development of the Saskatchewan river. We have had several speeches urging that at this session the government should bring down an item in the estimates which would indicate their intention of going ahead with the South Saskatchewan river project. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is in his place. He knows the province of Saskatchewan is very anxious to see this development proceeded with. They have agreed with him and with the P.F.R.A. officials to accept responsibility for their share of this project. One of the main reasons they are anxious to have it proceeded with immediately is the need for power in Saskatchewan. At the present time there is a real shortage of power. Owing to the rural electrification scheme introduced by the present government there has been a tremendous increase in the amount of power used.
The Budget-Mr. Wright
At the present time that power is developed mainly in two ways, from coal at Estevan and from crude oil through plants in centrally located areas. Their whole system has been set up with the idea of eventually using power from two developments on the Saskatchewan river, the first on the South Saskatchewan and the second at Fort a la Corne, just below where the two forks of the Saskatchewan join, north of Kinistino in northeastern Saskatchewan. An amount of approximately $1 million has been placed in the estimates for this development this year, but that will not be sufficient to get the South Saskatchewan project under way. The dam is going to be largely of earth, and it is estimated that it will take seven years to complete that part of the project and approximately ten years to complete the whole pregram of irrigation and power development. The cost to the federal government is estimated at between $68 and $69 million and to the provincial government somewhere between $34 and $35 million. If we are only going to spend $1 million as provided in the estimates this year it will take about 70 years to get the dam built, and I am afraid most of us, including the Minister of Agriculture, will not be very much interested in the matter then.
In my opinion this South Saskatchewan development is only a small part of the total development of that river. I think it necessary that this be gone ahead with first in order to control the flood waters of the Saskatchewan, but there is a further development at Fort a la Corne which will supply almost as much power as the South Saskatchewan project. Then if we go down to the estuary of the Saskatchewan and Carrot rivers we find, according to a survey made by the P.F.R.A. during the last two years, between three and four million acres of the best land to be found on the continent of North America. This is not in use today because of flood conditions. We do not have the figures of just how much money would be required to prevent this flooding, but I doubt if it would be as much as we are going to spend on the South Saskatchewan project. I doubt if it would cost $100 million to prevent the flooding which takes place in that area. If this flooding could be prevented through dams further up the Saskatchewan which would hold back the water, and if that area could be placed under cultivation, we would have not 500,000 or 750,000 acres of new land that could be irrigated under the South Saskatchewan project, but probably 3 to 4 million acres of the best land on this continent. As a result production in that
