The Budget-Mr. W. J. Browne area would be greatly increased'. Approximately two and a half to three million acres of this land lies in Manitoba and the remainder of almost a million acres in Saskatchewan. I am sure this is the largest single area of undeveloped land remaining in Canada, and it is probably one of the last large areas that can be opened up for development.
These are projects which should be developed. We all realize that with the present world situation we have to make large expenditures for defence; but if this country had maintained reasonable price controls we could have saved a large part of those expenditures. It is estimated that our defence budget this year will be approximately $1,600 million, and that in the next three years we are going to spend $5,000 million on defence projects. Anyone who will take the trouble to compare the prices we have to pay for equipment today with the prices we were paying in 1944 and 1945 will discover the startling fact that to buy airplanes and tanks today it costs the government approximately $3 for every $1 it cost in 1944. In other words if we had maintained some controls over prices and basic materials in this country we would have been able to get the same amount of war production for just one-third what we have to pay today. Then some of the money that could have been saved by reasonable controls in this country could have been spent on the development of new areas and the extension of railway lines, so that we would have been in a much better position to produce the sinews of war than is the case today.
I suggest to the government that while we are engaged in an effort to build a defence force that will work for peace, there are other projects which will also work for peace. The development of the food supplies of this country to the point where we had exportable surpluses that could be used to feed hungry peoples probably would be an even greater contribution to peace than our armed forces. Eventually we will have to realize that we cannot continue to have large areas of undeveloped territory while millions of people starve in the crowded countries of Asia. Only when we realize that and begin to develop our resources so that through their use we can supply some of the needs of the world will we be able to contribute effectively to peace.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. J. Browne (Si. John's West):
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to offer some observations of a general nature on some statements contained in the budget speech of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). I believe it is fair


to say that the good humoured appearance and manner of the minister in introducing his budget this year indicated that he did not find raising the necessary money a very difficult job. Anyone who examines the sources from which he is going to get his new taxes, $405 million, will see there are only half a dozen items from which he will get that large amount of money. It says something for the efficiency of the tax structure of Canada that such a great amount can be raised so simply.
The economic survey given by the minister draws attention, in my opinion, to the great influence which governments today have upon the direction and development of trade and commerce. Institutions like the wheat board, and legislation like the Agricultural Prices Support Act, the Fisheries Prices Support Act and the Agricultural Marketing Act, affect the prosperity of farmers and fishermen to a great extent. Controls and subsidies, taxes, duties and rates of exchange, can all be used by a minister of finance to bring about what he considers the best results for the people of this country.
It is startling to examine the figures given by the Minister of Finance in that respect. For example, he said that the action of the government in September, 1949, in altering exchange rates, had this effect: That the imports from the United Kingdom increased by 32 per cent; imports from countries other than the United States increased by 27 per cent; exports to the United States increased by 34 per cent; exports to the United Kingdom declined by 33 per cent. He said that trade was, in that way, balanced. I think we will all recognize that trade is a delicate thing when it is capable of such sudden and swift reversal. It happens that the way it went was all right, but if it had gone the other way the Minister of Finance would not have been in such good humour two weeks ago.
The remarkable increase in industrial activity in 1950, after the depressing start that we made last year, has resulted in increased earnings, increased profits, increased prices and, for the government, increased revenue. As the Minister of Finance would be the first to recognize, this increase was principally accounted for by the developments that took place last June when the North Korean forces invaded the south. It is remarkable how closely associated the country's prosperity seems to be with war. Of course, this is illusionary. While many people make profits out of war, those who are least able to bear the effects of war find that, as prices have gone up, their standard of living has been lowered. Whether this increase in Canada's

prosperity would have occurred but for the Korean affair is very problematical.
The minister draws attention to the increased productivity in European countries, and shows how they have expanded their production considerably in advance of what it was in 1939. To some extent the productivity of those countries during the past year is also attributable to war preparation. It is due, in large part, to the cumulative efforts of the aid which was distributed through the Marshall plan to those European countries whose recovery was considered to be necessary and desirable. Arrangements for this aid were made with the object of preserving those countries from falling under the influence of communism. So far as the United States itself is concerned, the effects of the Korean war in economic and commercial affairs have been greater than here. In the United States they have introduced a measure of price control, and there is reason, I believe, to feel that it is going to be successful.
Although in his speech the Minister of Finance indicated an appreciation of the menace of Russia to the free nations of the world, the policy of the government during the past year has shown only a fraction of the anxiety and fear that seem to be actuating the people and the government of the United States. It seems strange that these two countries, side by side and possessing the same knowledge of the dangers threatening the free world, should view this threat in such a different manner. The United States has taken most extreme measures to resist this threat. They have introduced compulsory military service, and are trying to conscript youths as early as eighteen years of age, whereas in this country we are going along dependent upon a half-hearted recruiting campaign to get 150,000 men in three years. At the conclusion of it we shall have in proportion about as many men as Belgium had in 1949.
When the armies of North Korea invaded South Korea last June, a quick victory by the communists was prevented only by the rapid action of the United States which was the only country possessing sufficient trained men to go to the assistance of the hard pressed South Korean forces. Canada had no troops to send. Three or four days after this aggression had occurred, parliament adjourned without having made any preparations for Canada to play its full part. Although Canada sent three ships of war, and gave other material help, it was unable to provide the ground forces which were most needed in that crisis. By the time the special session was called in September, the situation had become more grave but the 80709-148
23, 1951
The Budget-Mr. W. J. Browne government seemed to view the situation with no greater sense of urgency or concern. It is true that at that time powers were taken to raise money, and we did vote a large amount of money. Power was taken to recruit a special force for service wherever the United Nations wanted it to be sent. But here we are, ten months after the outbreak of the war, and Canada today has only one battalion in the field and 6,000 men en route.
I noticed that in a speech at Toronto the other night the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) said that people in the U.S.A. were complaining that Canada was not doing its share, because it was only doing one-twelfth or one-sixteenth when it should be doing more. He said, how is it no one says Argentina or Egypt is not contributing an equal share? I think it is due to the important position Canada has been playing in world affairs. Because of its actual wealth and its potential wealth, more is expected of Canada today than those countries which he mentioned. Our own deficiencies are reasons which should make us thankful that we are a neighbour of the United States. We receive protection from the United States that I do not think we fully appreciate. I am quite sure that if the United States were not there with its powerful forces there would be nothing to prevent Russia from attacking us instead of looking for objectives in Asia.
Not only those living in Canada but the whole world, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs has repeatedly said, owes a great debt to the United States. If it had not been for the decisive action of the United States in June, what would the United Nations have done? I contend that without the leadership of the United States there would be no United Nations today. If it had not been for the action of the United States, Korea would now be under communist control, and it is quite feasible that communist forces would have since invaded Formosa or even Japan. Because of the magnificent leadership of the United States in world affairs, I think it was rather surprising that the Secretary of State for External Affairs should speak as he recently did in Toronto. Some country must take the lead in upholding the principle of international justice and morality. What nation is better qualified to do so than the United States which, for several years past, has been distributing largess to all the nations of the world with a lavish hand from its vast resources? What nation today could equal the vast efforts she is making to rearm herself and protect the other nations of the world against aggression? What nation can say that the United States is doing less than her share for the maintenance

The Budget-Mr. W. J. Browne of world peace and the protection of the weaker freedom-loving nations of the world against aggression? There is no country so well qualified, for so many reasons, for the all-important task of world leadership. This is the role that the majority of nations have given to the United States today. The statesmen of other countries, whose contributions do not compare with those of the United States, I think should therefore refrain from publicly rebuking the United States for performing the duties which leadership of that nature requires.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs has complained about the criticism of Canada by people in the United States. He should remember that on at least three occasions in the past year the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent) did not hesitate to speak his mind quite frankly and quite firmly on subjects concerning the United States and on one occasion that I remember, whilst visiting the United States, the subject matter of his comments was of no apparent concern to Canada at all. If words have meanings, leadership implies followers who are filled with zeal and are loyal to the leader in the pursuit of those noble objectives of world peace and security and the social and economic progress of all the nations of the world. Such an attitude does not, of course, imply slavishness or obsequiousness. It seems to me that the discussion in Canadian forums, by cabinet ministers, of questions such as the unfavourable criticism of certain groups in- the United States is of doubtful value. It certainly seems to be far from the traditional idea we have had of the art of diplomacy. It seems to me that we are copying the bad example of the Russians who, by their brazen, openly aggressive and even insulting tactics, have made diplomacy so difficult today. Canadian public men it seems to me should not adopt those tactics. It is regrettable if they do; but that they should consider it necessary seems to show our helplessness in these difficult times, and the necessity for our depending upon God's help in the work which we have in hand.
For the success of the lofty undertakings entrusted to the United Nations more than diplomacy and ability is necessary today. I know that it is probably quite trite to say it, but everyone recognizes that we need the great virtues of patience, wisdom, charity and humility, and that we need to put our trust in God more than in guns. But throughout it all we need perseverance, keeping in sight the final aims we have in mind.
I am encouraged to offer these comments by some of the observations made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in his

speech in Toronto, when he said that foreign affairs are now the business of every Canadian family and the responsibility of every Canadian citizen. If such a statement applies equally to the citizens of the United States, I should like to hear his appraisal of the tremendously popular welcome given to General MacArthur on his return after his sudden dismissal from the high posts and the high offices which he has held because of the views which he had publicly expressed on the manner in which the Korean campaign had been carried on.
What are the aims of the United Nations? How many members of this house here tonight can tell what are the aims of the United Nations now in Korea? I do not believe anyone knows, not even my hon. friend the Minister of Veterans Affairs who represented Canada so well at the United Nations -this year. But I should like to draw attention to the statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs at the United Nations general assembly on September 27 last when- he laid down- five objectives that -the United Nations should -have. The first three of them -are as follows: First, a united and free Korea; second, assistance by the United Nations to the peoples of Korea in establishing peace and order throughout the territory of Korea; and third, a Korea not divided or disturbed by subversive communist elements directed from outside Korea.
Recent events seem to indicate a serious weakening in the resolution of the United Nations to attain these ends. Now no one hears any mention of a solution to the Korean problem at all that would require, for example, the aggressors to pay compensation for the damages and injuries they have inflicted upon the United Nations forces. Nevertheless, reparations of that kind seem to be imperative if international justice is to be respected. Those responsible for the conduct of the affairs of the United Nations should remember that it is desirable to have clear and definite aims and objectives. If these aims are always to be thwarted and negatived or neutralized by the fear of possible communist disapproval or action, then the work of the United Nations, in its most important aspect-the pursuit of peace and its maintenance-would be reduced to its lowest level. It would be better to reorganize the United Nations and proceed without the presence of Russia than always to have to submit to communist dictatorship and veto. For example, if Russia had happened to have judged the situation aright and to have been present at the security council at the time that the northern armies of Korea invaded southern Korea, I think that she would have been far more successful. It was only the

absence of Russia from the security council that permitted the measures to be taken which resulted in the defeat of North Korea.
To one who comes from a country which owes the loss of its independence to the inability of finance ministers to balance its budget for a number of years, the ease with which the Minister of Finance accomplished his task is a source of great astonishment. I realize that Canada in the early thirties was also having its financial difficulties and its budget remained unbalanced for many years. But during the war the revenues increased and if it had not been for the extraordinary war expenditures, the excess of revenues over expenditures would have been great.
The potential wealth of this country is amazing. Under the very walls of this building the mighty Ottawa river flowing majestically to join the St. Lawrence is already, to the people of Ontario and Quebec, a great source of electrical energy and power and is capable of producing even greater quantities of electrical energy and power. The mighty St. Lawrence river could prove to be an immense reservoir of electrical energy; and in my opinion the wealth and production of those two provinces are closely associated with the fact that they possess within their borders this great source and cause of wealth. The growth and prosperity of Montreal, Toronto and the cities and towns adjacent to the hydroelectric developments are due in great measure to the availability of the supply of electrical energy. I should like to see the St. Lawrence waterways project become a reality. Yet I sympathize with the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) and the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan) for the anxiety which they feel lest the deepening of the St. Lawrence and the development of the canal system should spell further decline for the maritime provinces. It seems to be understood by them-and I believe their opinion is generally shared by the members in all parties from the maritimes-that the maritime provinces will decline in proportion as the central provinces improve their financial and economic position. This should not be so, and it should not be beyond the wisdom of the statesmen of this country to investigate the cause of these fears and dispel them. It is a remarkable thing to me, who came into confederation just a couple of years ago, to find that after 84 years of confederation the members from the maritimes rise in their places and speak of the mistake that was made as if it had been only yesterday. They feel so bitterly that today they question the advisability of this vast project which seems to be full of benefits for Canada as a whole.

Browne I can only re-echo the sentiments expressed by the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Balcom) in his speech today, on which I also congratulate him, when he said that he could not see how something which was going to be of general benefit to Canada as a whole should be of disadvantage for any considerable part of it. It seems to me, however, that the government should take these matters into consideration seriously and do all in their power to alleviate the injustices of which the members from the maritimes complain.
It was remarked in the Turgeon report that the central provinces had no complaints or questions to ask about the freight rates that prevailed in Ontario or Quebec. That was a significant fact. It showed that it did not matter which way the freight rates went, Ontario and Quebec would be prosperous anyhow. I know that by union of Newfoundland with Canada the economy of Newfoundland has been seriously affected, and with a view to putting that economy on a sounder basis I have repeatedly drawn the attention of this house, and especially of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), to the promotion of agriculture in Newfoundland. I have tried to induce him to come down and visit us, but he has not yet found it convenient to do so. He is such an expert on such a matter that I believe it would be helpful to us if he did find it convenient to come.
I have great faith in Newfoundland. I think that it can produce a far greater share of the food and the clothing that it needs if agriculture is properly developed. Agriculture is a subject that comes especially within the duties of the federal government, and I do not think it is fair for the federal government to leave so much of the solution of this great economic problem to the greatly handicapped department of agriculture in Newfoundland. They have only one or two officials down there. They have not got the experts in all departments that the federal government has. I would plead with the Minister of Agriculture again this year that he come to see us and see for himself our possibilities, and see if he cannot give us greater help than we have yet received from the federal government.
Somewhat different considerations apply to the question of the fisheries. In the remarks that I made on the speech from the throne I urged the government of Canada to do in Newfoundland as they had done in Nova Scotia, namely, send a man down there to organize the fishermen. Well, I do not know whether the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. W. J. Browne Mayhew) took my remarks seriously when I spoke about what had happened in 1929 when the government of Canada engaged the Rev. Dr. Coady, the great co-operative expert, to go around Nova Scotia and organize the fishermen of that province. He did so. and the united maritime fishermen is the result. It is a very powerful organization today. Whether the Minister of Fisheries took me seriously or not, it appears that the premier of Newfoundland took the matter very seriously, because he has done the very thing that I recommended. He called a convention of fishermen. A delegation of 200 fishermen came to St. John's to a convention at the government's expense. He brought Dr. Coady from Nova Scotia to lecture the delegates on the benefits of co-operation, and on the advantages that would come to them if they would organize and market their products co-operatively and also buy their goods on a co-operative basis.
When I was speaking in the same debate I made some statements on the prices received by fishermen to which the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Carter) called attention the other day. It must have been fairly obvious to anyone who read my speech-and I am sure it was to the Minister of Fisheries-that when I was speaking about the prices paid to fishermen by the merchants I was not condemning all the merchants of Newfoundland. I was speaking only of course from information which I had gathered from those who had come to see me, and those with whom I had come in contact. But even then I found some fish buyers and merchants paying higher prices than others. I was criticizing those whose prices appeared to be unreasonable. Now a royal commission has been appointed in Newfoundland to investigate these prices and the fisheries prices support board is also doing the same thing. Therefore I think that further comment should be deferred until one or both of these bodies have reported.
On former occasions I have brought to the attention of this house the inadequacy of the financial terms that Newfoundland received on union, and I have asked the government to act in accordance with the terms of union and appoint a royal commission to go into that question in regard to Newfoundland. The term of union which deals with this subject reads as follows:
In view of the difficulty of predicting with sufficient accuracy the financial consequences to Newfoundland of becoming a province of Canada, the government of Canada will appoint a royal commission within eight years from the date of union to review the financial position of the province of Newfoundland and to recommend the form and


scale of additional financial assistance, if any, that may be required by the government of the province of Newfoundland to enable it to continue public services at the levels and standards reached subsequent to the date of union, without resorting to taxation more burdensome, having regard to capacity to pay, than that obtaining generally in the region comprising the maritime provinces of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, and Prince Edward Island.
That section gave a term of eight years within which this royal commission should be appointed; but it has been my opinion from the beginning that the financial terms have been inadequate. Since, sir, the commission of government left a legacy of between $40 million and $50 million, of which about half has now been expended in two years, and the government of Newfoundland has been depending upon a transitional grant of $6J- million and drawing about $12 million a year from the surplus, it will be seen that in another two years Newfoundland will be in serious financial stress again, and as only the other day one of the ministers in the provincial government, namely, the minister of natural resources, resigned and said that in his opinion the policy of the government was driving Newfoundland into financial ruin, I believe the government of Canada should soon give consideration to the appointment of such a royal commission.
The Newfoundland government has been working with feverish energy to try and induce foreign capital to come into the province, but apart from the development on the Quebec-Labrador frontier no foreign capital has yet been invested in Newfoundland. The government of Newfoundland, however, out of the surplus, has started four enterprises of an industrial nature. They are building a cement plant and two plants for the production of gypsum products, and near St. John's they are building a mill to treat birch. The initiative for the appointment of this royal commission, it seems to me, rests with the government of Canada, as the government will have to bear the reproaches of Newfoundlanders. I hate to think what Newfoundlanders will be saying in eighty-four years' time about what happened in 1949. I think the government of Canada should consider the question now and not allow it to become a running sore. The government should show its sincerity and interest in the new province, because the problem is a very serious one. We should not have to depend upon socialistic enterprise, in which I am sure the federal government has very little faith.
The Minister of Finance remarked that the action taken by members of the North Atlantic treaty organization to protect themselves had been a great and incalculable change for

the better during the last year. The prolonged negotiations between the governments of Belgium, Holland, Luxembourg, France and western Germany in regard to the integration of the coal and steel industry terminated since the minister brought down his budget. I am sure however that he will agree that this arrangement is a matter of tremendous importance. There is reason to hope that the arrangement will mean lasting peace between these two countries, France and Germany, which have been at war so often in the last one hundred years. It seems to mean more than that; it means that these two countries will collaborate in the common defence of western civilization, which has been in such mortal peril during the last few months.
The underlying causes of these actions are due to the fear of communist aggression from Russia. There has been a general appreciation that there is no time to lose on the part of the western nations. They must unite in resistance to this hateful, inhuman thing which is opposed to everything that Christian men hold dear. The governments of western Europe and of the western world generally know the tremendous issues that are at stake -the dignity of man and the Christian conception of the importance of the individual, parliamentary government and freedom itself.
The preservation of this priceless heritage justifies the greatest sacrifices on the part of free men everywhere. For that reason members of all parties in the house have refrained from criticism of the government in raising the money necessary to carry out defence projects. Where we differ from the government is in the impact which this new tax will have upon the people of Canada. It is a principle of taxation that those best able to bear the burden should be the ones who would have to carry it. The very rich corporations, the very rich people should have to pay far more in proportion than those who are barely getting along, hand to mouth. It is a criticism which I think is justified, that in these few taxes, which seem so simple, imposeu the other day by the Minister of Finance, he has given another boost to the rise in the cost of living. And, as the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley) has so well said, it is the people of low incomes who are going to feel most the effects of this new taxation.
The increased sales tax and taxes on stoves, refrigerators and washing machines will be felt most by those who are least able to bear the added cost. Today these items can scarcely be regarded as luxuries, in a country which has so much electrical energy as has Canada. To the harassed housewife, the mother of several children, it seems to me
The Budget-Mr. Sinnott that the washing machine is a godsend; and to put a tax on that is simply to prevent her and her young family from having that advantage, and seems to be imposing a hardship on those who are least able to bear it.
We can only hope that the criticisms the minister has received from all quarters in the house in respect of putting on these taxes will have some effect upon him in the future. As he deemed it advisable two weeks ago to reduce the tax on candy from 30 to 15 per cent, we can only hope that he may come to the conclusion that, after all, perhaps it is better to put a little extra tax on liquor, or on some other articles better able to carry them than the ones I have already mentioned.
The minister has mentioned that we have two things in mind, two great issues, namely the pursuit of peace and the control of inflation. In the pursuit of peace the government should take care that the standard of living of which Canada has been so proud should not be allowed to deteriorate. There is grave fear that in its methods of attaining peace it may fail to control inflation, which we all fear so much.

Mr. Speaker, we are living at a time so critical in the history of our country and of civilization that no one with any proper sense of responsibility should allow himself to be critical just for the sake of trying to score an advantage. How has this difficult situation arisen? Has it just "growed" like Topsy? Let me review it very briefly. After the unfreezing of prices and abandonment of subsidies which came after the last war, prices rose from 119 in 1945 to 123 in 1946, to 135 in 1947, to 155 in 1948, and to 167 in 1950.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

Disgraceful is right when you have not found any solution from a man like that who makes that kind of speech. Then he goes on to say:
As I say, the government persisted in this technique, which was designed for a depression, long after it was made clear that there was a boom. As I have mentioned in this house before, the Winnipeg Free Press referred to this as the big blunder; while the Hamilton Spectator, in rather racy language, referred to it as the disastrous holiday-mood easy-money era that found politicians and economic pressure groups doing everything in their power to make inflation a permanent institution.
Previous to this parliament the policy of the Conservative party was to have all controls abolished. When those controls were taken off then the party seems to be divided as to whether or not they should all be put back on. There is no consistency whatever in their arguments.
Then I should like to refer to the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), whom I consider one of the brightest members of the opposition. After listening to him speak the other evening for forty-five minutes we were still at a loss to know just what suggestions were being made to the government to cure the inflationary trend. Then we go to the bright and would-be leader of the opposition, the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker). Here is his contribution, as reported on page 1919 of Hansard of April 11:
Mr. Speaker, I have sat here through the debate waiting to hear the answer to the question that the

Canadian people are asking: what is the government going to do about the high cost of living? What is going to be done about inflation? What measures are to be taken? For two days this discussion has proceeded, and as yet there is no suggestion that anything effective is to be done to meet a situation that affects every home in the country. No proof is needed that inflation today is terrible in its incidence and effect. No one expects the government to do everything, but at least the people as a whole have a right to expect that the government will do something at this time.
I would say that that was a pretty sensible speech, but after following it over the next two or three pages 1 find that there is not one solitary effort made to tell the government what to do to bring down the cost of living. Then we heard from the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth (Mr. Charlton) but he made no suggestions. Then we heard from the flaming hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson), who gave one of his great oratorical efforts tonight. We are all pleased to hear his humour. In one breath he was saying that the government was all wrong, that there should be private enterprise, and then he was saying that the government should get out of business. How can you make sense out of two statements like that?

Britain's Imports
One big element in the cost of living, the prices we have to pay for imports, is outside the control of the government.

I am quite in accord with the hon. member for Hamilton West that something should be done about this inflationary trend; but in all the speeches we have heard in this house, both from the opposition and this side, there have not been many suggestions as to how government expenditure could be cut. I think the only hon. member to make a suggestion of that kind was the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Dupuis); and I think if the hon. member could go into the various real estate transactions that have taken place over the years he would find that the lawyers skimmed1 the cream off those. Just recently I read an article in a Toronto newspaper about a court case that had been adjourned six times, and the judge said the reason for all the adjournments was that the lawyers were making so much money out of real estate they did not have time for petty cases.
What I am going to suggest may not meet with the approval of everyone here, but I think it will meet with the approval of the hon. member for Hamilton West. I say that the essentials of life should be subsidized, such as bread, meat and milk. To pay for such subsidies money would have to be found; and while I am suggesting to the government that these subsidies should be paid I am also going to tell 1hem where the money can be found.

The Budget-Mr. Sinnott The hon. member for Coast-Capilano was careful in his remarks today in dealing with the tax on liquor, but I am going to propose a tax of 2 cents an ounce on all hard liquor over and above the present tax, a tax of 1 cent an ounce on wine, and a special tax on beer by the glass.

I was Johnny on the spot
when the vote was taken. There is something that can be done. If the government would allow the people to keep something instead of taking it all away in taxes we would have plenty of production. Now, when I say what I have to say I hope it will be taken in a friendly way by the cabinet. However, what I propose to say, Mr. Speaker, is not what the opposition thinks at all. During the last war, with the taxation as high as it was at that time, labour in this country refused to work because most of their earnings were taken away by their employers at the end of the month.

After very careful thought I say that subsidies are necessary, but they are only temporary. They are only necessary temporarily for the simple reason that if you


allow production to run its course it will overtake this inflationary trend. I have indicated the way in which the government could dig up some of the money, and since there are sixteen members of the cabinet I suppose they can dig up some somewhere else.
I propose now that, in 1951, the producers of this country be given a concession in their taxes to the extent of 75 per cent of the amount they produce over and above what they produced in 1950. In 1952 I would propose to give them a reduction of 75 per cent of what they produced over and above 1951. In 1953 I would propose to give them a reduction of 75 per cent of what they produced over and above 1952. This would give the producers of this country and the farmers of this country some incentive to go to work. When the producers of this country realize that they are at least going to have some remuneration for themselves if they produce more than they produced the year before, I am sure we will receive the cooperation of all the producers of this country, both in the factories and on the farm, and this inflationary trend could be stopped in that way.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance

I am told by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sinclair) that I am perfectly right. I know, Mr. Speaker, that production and work is the only solution. I listened the other night while the member for Oxford (Mr. Murray) quoted the nineteenth verse of the third chapter of Genesis which says:
In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground.
Mr. Speaker, he should have gone on a little further and said: If thou wilt not work, thou shalt not eat.
I have indicated that production is the only solution to this inflationary trend. If the government will only allow the producers of this country to take hold, and will show them a three-year program, I am sure that those who produce the beef and the hogs, those who produce the essentials of life, will do the job themselves.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after all those speeches dealing with the budget introduced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), certainly our Liberal friends, weary of all these criticisms, are wondering what now can be said against the the budget. It may be that I will add nothing new to this discussion. Nevertheless, I feel

it is my duty, in times as serious as these, to express what I know to be the feelings of the people of Labelle constituency.
Moreover, I wish to state, officially and categorically, my opposition to such a budget, knowing as I do what great difficulties and responsibilities rest on those who, today, let the government impose such a heavy burden of taxes on the people, without proclaiming their refusal to approve the measure introduced, without proclaiming their refusal to follow the government in the nefarious road they are taking.
If so many speeches have been made against the budget it is because protests have come from every quarter.
It was not necessary for me to travel across the length and breadth of my constituency to find out the views of my constituents in this matter. The very first people I met, whether their political affiliation was Liberal or Conservative, all expressed the same opinion: this is a disastrous budget, a depressing budget, one which makes us consider the future with the greatest misgivings.
In any event, I have received very many letters that would have certainly enlightened me had there been any need for that. Certain people are really discouraged. Up to now, it was all they could do to make ends meet, in spite of all their sacrifices. But now the taxes they have to pay are going up constantly, as well as the cost of living. A large number of those who have families to provide for are most concerned about this situation. I can readily understand their, misgivings.
In spite of all that, one of my constituents, probably trying to find something humorous in this rather than cry over it-I must say though that he is a bachelor-wrote to me about the budget:
So far cartoonists have depicted the taxpayer as a man to whom the authorities have left only a barrel so that he will not be indecent. I rather think now that the new taxes will have done away with the barrel itself; we are being deprived of what little we had left. You will admit that that is becoming indecent.
With or without a barrel the taxpayer is in for a rough time. Some time ago the government tried to apply the policy known in the United States as a "soak-the-rich" policy. And the rich paid, so much so that there are hardly any of them left. And today we find that in trying to do away with the capitalists we have not done away with the very poor. On the contrary, overtaxing the rich has been harmful to a great many poor.
23, 1351
The Budget-Mr. Courtemanche
However, all that is ancient history now, since that well has run dry and it has been found necessary to turn to the man with a moderate income, a very moderate income, and even to the poor, to tax them on every little necessity they buy. For a good part of the day the worker and the farmer work only to pay taxes, to fill up the treasury. It is better not to try to figure out the amount of taxes we pay on any one dollar article, for the answer would leave us greatly discouraged.
Some may say: What about defence? I am all for the defence of Canada, but I am a little less enthusiastic about the defence of Korea. However, the defence of Canada or Korea does not imply that we should ruin our country. Some will say that our way of life, our institutions, our democracy are at stake. It is precisely because we must save all those things that we should not fight our enemy on the one hand and give him arms and munitions on the other.
By overtaxing the people, by refusing to take any steps to curb inflation, we are supplying arms and munitions to those we claim to be fighting in Korea or elsewhere. Inflation, let us never forget it, will always be a powerful weapon in the hands of our enemy. If the communists found it so easy to control China, it was largely due to inflation, to soaring prices. It is to be deeply regretted that our leaders do not understand that or act as though they did not understand it.
If it is really a matter of defending our country, the task surely becomes complicated, if not impossible, because of these tremendous imposts and of the fantastic rise in prices.
I beg permission to read extracts from articles on these new taxes, which appeared in two French-language weeklies. One is Notre Temps, the other Le Front Ouvrier, two publications aimed at two different classes of readers.
This is what Mr. Fernand Bourret writes in he Front Ouvrier:
The burden of war expenditures will be borne by the taxpayers, through the payment of all kinds of taxes. If the present basis of taxation were modified, it would be possible perhaps to lighten some people's burden, but in the main, however, the taxes made necessary by our war spending are impoverishing the country and reducing our standard of welfare.
The freezing of prices might make it possible to relieve the pain caused by the high cost of living.
2312	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Courtemanche
Such relief however would only be temporary, and the pain would again be sharply felt as soon as the analgesic had lost its effectiveness.
The high living costs due to heavy taxes, ever-increasing government expenditures, undue profits, combines and restrictions of all kinds which slow up production and keep prices from going down, can only be remedied through concerted efforts, especially as regards war spending.
Here is now the opinion expressed by Mr. J. T. Larochelle in Notre Temps. Let us see first what he has to say on the sales tax:
An important point the minister has not cared to stress is the pyramiding of the sales tax which is bound to occur in connection with a great number of commodities in current use. This tax is levied on raw materials, on the semi-manufactured product and finally on the finished product. Thus it is levied as much as three or four times (according to the number of taxable transactions) in greater amount every time before the product finally reaches the consumer. In most cases therefore the official increase from 8 to 10 per cent will, in fact, be much greater than suggested by the minister, the proportion varying according to the commodities.
In other words, we have a pyramid. And what a pyramid! That is why, a moment ago, we said it might be better if we did not try to find out the tax content of the dollar we earn and spend,
Although I do not necessarily share all Mr. Larochelle's opinions, here are the conclusions he draws in Notre Temps:
One must conclude that, in deciding upon new taxes, the Minister of Finance and the government have not taken into account the general interest and the economic conditions brought about by our military effort. Far from curbing inflation and the increase in the cost of living, they have levied taxes which, they admit, threaten to entail a large increase in the cost of essential goods. In the general calculations of the budgetary estimates, they have even speculated on an increase of approximately 5 per cent. The increase in taxes, like the rise in prices,-and the latter may easily climb by 10 per cent within a year,-entails no real sacrifice except for families already living on a small or moderate income, the very families that should be spared, while limited companies, whose profits are increasing and will continue to increase as a result of military contracts and inflation, are on the whole, being spared.
I do not agree with the author in the closing sentence of his article because I believe that, except in a few cases, limited companies, whose shareholders are very often people in the low income groups, people with small savings, will be very hard hit by these new taxes.
Be that as it may, these two responsible newspapers do not hesitate to condemn the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance. In so doing, they only reflect the opinion of both the urban and the rural population. There is no point in deluding ourselves: the people are angry, very angry in fact, because they feel let down by their
IMr. Courtemanche.]

own government. It is not surprising that in trade union circles there is talk of requesting wage increases which would inevitably bring about higher prices. But all workers do not belong to trade unions. Farmers, for instance, are not affiliated to any of them; yet the cost of living has dealt them such a blow that they wonder what the future holds in store for them.
One aspect of the budget, however, has not been sufficiently stressed. It is a provocative budget not only because of its harshness but also because of its presentation. The government raises taxes while claiming that it wishes to curb inflation. And once these increased taxes have boosted the cost of living still higher, the people are asked to economize on a larger scale.
I know that, during their election campaigns, the hon. members opposite are in the habit of making all kinds of promises they soon forget. I must also admit that quite often, and too often in my opinion, the electors do not hold it against them unduly.
Yet I feel that, where a new series of taxes is concerned, the people are not such good fellows, nor are they so naive. According to an old saying, the pill has been sugar-coated. That is all very well but it is quite another matter to give the impression that there is no pill at all and that both the coating and the inside are exactly the same. Since we are on the subject of pills, that is one the people will not swallow.
When he was told last year that taxes would not be raised the hon. the Postmaster General (Mr. Rinfret) expressed his gratitude to the Minister of Finance, stating openly that higher taxes would have increased inflation. It is utter nonsense today to try to make us believe that taxes are being increased in order to stop inflation. The Minister of Finance acts indeed, Mr. Speaker, as though he wanted us to experience the worst inflationary conditions.
Has any thought been given to the dire consequences of inflation, which the new taxes will help along? Has any consideration been given to the widow who thought she had no reason to dread the future and who finds out now that the value of the insurance she lives on has decreased by about 50 per cent. Have the disastrous effects of inflation on a multitude of thrifty people been taken into consideration? Has any thought been given to the fact that it would

discourage saving? Apparently not, for after the imposition of all these taxes, surtaxes and overtaxes, people are being urged to save.
Of course I am in favour of saving. But one should not try to make the taxpayer believe that he must or can save with the budget of the Minister of Finance.
I know that the minister is surrounded and advised by learned experts and by economists with stacks of diplomas. I am afraid however that these learned experts, these distinguished economists do not come down often enough from their ivory tower. Their work is apparently limited to somewhat abstract calculations. I appreciate their learning. I would not dare contradict an astronomer who would tell me that the earth is so many miles from the moon. But there is someone who is able to contradict the learned experts of the Minister of Finance and I refer to the Canadian housewife who cannot be satisfied with mathematical calculations but has to do the buying for the family and realizes that her husband's earnings, though they may sometimes seem increased, are no longer sufficient to feed, clothe and house the family.
I wish the experts would spend a little time asking questions of the man in the street to find out how he reacts. Naturally, such is not their responsibility. And I know that some experts in England were offended one day when someone took it upon himself to blame them and tell them that their plans were not practicable. One of them replied that "he did not care whether his plans would work out or not." His job was simply to set them up. Having talked, a few days ago, with a few immigrants recently arrived from Great Britain, I got the impression that the British experts were leading their country to the very brink of disaster, if not to complete ruin.
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make it clear that the Canadian taxpayer has no intention of being led as the British people are being led and have been led for the past few years. If we had wanted socialism, we would have elected our friends of the C.C.F.; if we had wanted a receipt instead of a pay envelope, we would have elected representatives of socialism. This is not what happened, however, and as things stand at the moment I am afraid the C.C.F. will claim before long that the Liberals have stolen their platform. It is true that socialists have been said to be
23. 1951
The Budget-Mr. Courtemanche merely Liberals in a hurry. That was some time ago and it might be that today the Liberals, without hurrying, have nevertheless caught up with the socialists.
But let us come back to the budget and the new taxes. Have its repercussions on the provincial and municipal authorities and the school boards been considered? The premier of Quebec has already complained, and rightly so, that more than 77 per cent of all revenues in Canada were collected by the Ottawa government, leaving only 22 per cent to the provinces, municipal corporations and school boards. That situation has not been improved by the Minister of Finance when he devised those new taxes, and the way things are being done, this government in Ottawa is going to have a new monopoly on taxation.
We know that the centralists have not abandoned their projects or their schemes. Since they cannot succeed by constitutional amendments or by any such means, they are undoubtedly contriving to starve the provinces. What they say runs somewhat as follows:	"We will not tamper with your
rights; have no fear. We will be satisfied with depriving you of your income!" Now, of what value are rights without powers or sources of taxation?
Indeed, it must not be forgotten that taxation cannot be carried out indefinitely, without ill effects. If it is overdone as it was in the new budget, where will it lead us?
The Calgary Herald at one time published an article which reads as follows:
Let us harbour no illusions about income taxes. They penalize industry, and penalize brains. The skilled, enterprising man who really contributes to the material welfare of society is being victimized. The greater his abilities and the more he uses them, the more money he has to pay the government.
Under the present taxation system in Canada it does not pay to work hard, to be intelligent, to produce. Thousands of Canadians, in all income brackets, escape taxation in a way that is perfectly legal and honest; they work less than they could, produce less than they could, earn less than they could. They pay less taxes but, in so doing, produce less.
The damage wrought by this behaviour is infinitely greater than that caused by any other attitude. Throwing people into prison is no remedy.
But what are we to say today, now that we have a surtax on income tax? A government supporter has stated that we should produce more. But who is going to ruin his health or neglect his family or forgo all leisure just to pay higher taxes? If the

The Budget-Mr. Courtemanche key to freedom is to be found in production, let us encourage and not stifle production.
If Isocrates were still alive he would surely repeat that those who make money are considered as criminals because they are more harshly penalized than real criminals.
To my mind income tax is the most harmful of all forms of taxation, because it stifles initiative and discourages those who are industrious and active. It is unnecessary, I hope, to repeat that this income tax is especially hard on people of low income. Gone are the days when only rich men suffered from this tax. Nowadays if one manages to stay alive and to dress in a halfdecent way, one is sure to be the butt of the traditional April fool's joke perpetrated by the Minister of Finance, by the present incumbent as well as by those who have preceded him in that office.
This income tax surcharge cannot be justified. As far as its repercussions are concerned, they will certainly be disastrous.
But, some will say, it is luxuries that are taxed. Let us have a look at these luxuries. Washing machines, refrigerators, automobiles? Of course, they may, at times, be luxury items but generally they are daily essentials. For many people, a car is a means of livelihood. It is essential to a good many people. Now these items are taxed beyond all limits.
Cigarettes too are luxury items, according to the minister's experts. Personally, I do not think so, although I do not smoke. Whether we like it or not, this new tax will only encourage smuggling. Of course, the police will keep a closer watch at customs ports, but even then there will be more smuggling than ever before in the history of this country. We see in the papers that already important seizures have been made. But everybody knows that they represent only a very small part of the actual smuggling going on.
That may well bring about a large decrease in the government's revenues, in spite of the tax increase. But what worries me more is that our people are once again tempted to resort to fraud, illegal practices and dishonesty. In my opinion, that is even more serious than the rest. We have not forgotten the wartime black market, and we also know of a certain grey market in building materials. Let us not delude ourselves. Nearly


everybody had a hand in the pie and nearly everyone has disregarded and defrauded our laws. Prohibition had disastrous consequences in the United States, not so much in loss of government revenue as on account of the deplorable state of mind it induced. Excessive taxes on cigarettes will inevitably have the same results. In Ottawa, in Montreal and nearly everywhere in Canada people are smoking more American cigarettes than ever before. We have no right to kill an industry and, more particularly, we have no right to prompt people to act illegally.
As far as the new sales tax is concerned, or rather the increase of the existing tax, it is what I would call an underhand tax, a too well hidden tax, which lets the customer believe that the shopkeeper is making an undue profit, when it is the federal government which taxes, one after the other, all the raw materials and finally the finished product. A pyramid, I said a moment ago, a pyramid which unfortunately reflects no great credit on our times. That 10 per cent tax will, more than any other, increase the cost of living. If the 8 per cent tax was a factor of the high cost of living, what will be the effect of that increase to 10 per cent?
And it is the same thing, sir, for all the new taxes or the tax increases contained in the new budget. Of course, taxes are necessary and new taxes always meet with criticism. However common sense should prevail and I think that this time the government has gone too far. The government make's a pretext of defence to go on a spending spree, to incur wartime as well as peacetime expenses which, far from strengthening our position, may very well weaken it to the point where our enemies will gloat over it.
The government wants to play the part of a great power and for that reason is inconsiderately taxing the people. Let us not forget the fable of the frog that wanted to be as big as the ox. The Minister of Finance could have been less exacting without endangering the defence of our country. On the contrary by not endangering our way of life as he is now doing the minister would have only strengthened the belief of the people in the value of the present system.
For all those reasons, I consider that the budget strikes a hard blow not only at the economy of the nation, but also at the defence of our country.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that if there is one thing that the budget and the proposals for raising additional taxes which have been laid before the house by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) revealed, and if there is one thing above all others which the reaction to the budget throughout the country revealed, it is the necessity at which we have arrived in this country of making a real and genuine effort to reduce non-essential government expenditures.
I am not one who lacks confidence in the Canadian economy, or confidence in the willingness of the Canadian people, and their ability to bear any proper load which may be placed upon them; but I say we have reached the point when the interests of the Canadian people and the welfare of the Canadian economy demand that, at a time when they are being asked-and properly-to bear the heavy load of defence expenditures, they should be relieved of the load of unnecessary and extravagant governmental waste.
It is true, with respect to the increases in taxes the Minister of Finance has outlined in his budget, and it is true with respect to the extra revenues the minister says he has to raise, that we have inflation, which of itself produces or, in the past, has had the effect of producing about twice the surplus for which the minister has budgeted over the years-and will probably do the same again this year. But that very inflation and the increased cost of living which it imposes upon the Canadian people make it essential that we reduce our expenditures so that those taxes which bear on the cost of living and which, in fact, increase the cost of living, will not be necessarily increased simply as the result of spending such as we find taking place at the present time in many fields, if we examine the details of the estimates for this year.
The burden of defence preparedness is another factor which makes it so much more essential even than it was in the past that we should reduce unessential expenditures. After all, last year the Minister of Finance told us in his budget speech of March 28 that we had at that time reached the limit of buoyant revenues, reached the point beyond which any increased expenditure would have to be provided for out of increased taxation.
That being the case, then how much more essential it becomes, when we are faced with
The Budget-Mr. Fulton a burden over the next few years of several billions of dollars of increased expenditures, that we should search for and find and insist upon the reduction of non-essential expenditures. The parliamentary assistant emphasized this point in his speech this afternoon. He emphasized the point made on March 28 last year by the Minister of Finance when, as reported at page 1216 of Hansard, he said:
The conclusion then which I reach is that no minister of finance in the foreseeable future will have an easier task than I have, namely, that of covering about $2,400 million of expenditure.
In other words he was saying there that it is not foreseeable that in future years we will have a level of expenditure below $2,400 million. Mr. Speaker, $2,400 million is what the government was asking a nation of from 12 to 14 millions of people to undertake, apart altogether from defence expenditures, as the level of spending of the federal government alone.
This leads me to the point where I think we should accept the challenge which was issued in the past by the Minister of Finance and repeated this afternoon by the parliamentary assistant to suggest some positive way in which the government could make economies. I find it interesting to note that for the second time in this session the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sinclair) appears to be more concerned with showing how difficult it is to reduce expenditures and spends far more time pointing out why we cannot reduce expenditures than he spends in really trying to find out how we can reduce expenditures. Again I suggest that if he would bend the same energies to finding possible economies as he does to justifying the extravagance of the government we might hope for a more equitable burden of taxation on the Canadian people.
Since it is close to eleven o'clock and 1 intend to discuss some details in this connection I should like to move the adjournment of the debate.
Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.
